species.name: Ramps (wild leeks)
species.habitat: Rich, moist hardwood forest — maple, beech and basswood slopes, often in large colonies.
species.identify: Two or three smooth, flat, lily-like leaves rising from a single reddish stalk, and an unmistakable onion-garlic smell when crushed. If it does not smell of onion, it is not a ramp.
species.use: Leaves in eggs, pesto and butter. Cut one leaf per plant and leave the bulb — colonies take seven years to replace a dug bulb.
species.lookalikes: Lily of the valley and false hellebore grow in the same woods and are toxic. Neither smells of onion; false hellebore has pleated, ribbed leaves.
species.caution: Over-harvested across the east; Quebec restricts picking and sale. Take a few leaves, never the patch.

species.name: Fiddleheads (ostrich fern)
species.habitat: Floodplains, riverbanks and damp woods, usually in stands.
species.identify: Tight bright-green coils with a deep U-shaped groove on the inside of a smooth stem, wrapped in papery brown scales that rub off. No fuzz.
species.use: Rinse well and boil at least 15 minutes or steam 12 — never raw or lightly sautéed. Then butter and lemon.
species.lookalikes: Only ostrich fern is eaten. Bracken (carcinogenic), cinnamon and interrupted ferns are woolly or round-stemmed, and wood ferns are shaggy with scales. Lady fern is the close double: it also has papery scales and a U-shaped groove, so check for ostrich fern's stiff, dark brown fertile fronds from last year standing in the clump. If it isn't smooth with that groove, leave it.
species.caution: Raw or undercooked fiddleheads cause food poisoning. Take no more than half the coils from a crown.

species.name: Morels
species.habitat: Dying elms and old apple orchards in the east; burned conifer forest in the west; river bottoms everywhere.
species.identify: Honeycomb pitted cap fused to the stem, and completely hollow from cap tip to stem base when sliced lengthwise.
species.use: Always cooked. Halve, rinse out the grit, sauté in butter.
species.lookalikes: False morels (Gyromitra) have a brain-like wrinkled cap and are cottony or chambered inside, not hollow. They can be fatal.
species.caution: Slice every single one lengthwise before it goes in the basket.

species.name: Stinging nettle
species.habitat: Rich disturbed ground, old barnyards, streambanks, hedgerows.
species.identify: Opposite, deeply toothed, heart-based leaves on a square stem, covered in stinging hairs. The sting is the identification.
species.use: Gloves and scissors; take the top four leaves of young plants. Cooking or soaking takes away the sting. Soup, tea, anywhere spinach goes.
species.lookalikes: Wood nettle stings too — it has alternate leaves where stinging nettle's are opposite. Clearweed looks similar but has no stinging hairs and a translucent stem. Neither is dangerous; the sting is how you know you have a nettle.

species.name: Dandelion
species.habitat: Lawns, meadows, roadside edges — anywhere the ground has been disturbed.
species.identify: A basal rosette of jagged, backward-pointing lobes, a hollow leafless stalk with milky sap, and one flower per stalk.
species.use: Young leaves before flowering are least bitter; flowers for fritters and wine; roots roasted.
species.lookalikes: Cat's ear and hawkweed are hairy and harmless. Avoid sprayed lawns rather than avoiding the plant.

species.name: Wild asparagus
species.habitat: Fence lines, ditches and railway embankments — escaped from old gardens.
species.identify: In spring, familiar spears. Find the patch in fall instead: tall feathery ferns with red berries mark exactly where to return.
species.use: Snap the spear where it breaks cleanly. Take a few per crown and leave the rest to fern out.
species.lookalikes: Pick spears only where you can see last year's dry asparagus stalks or where you saw the feathery ferns. The red berries on mature ferns are not edible.

species.name: Spruce and fir tips
species.habitat: Any spruce or true fir you can name; roadside trees at eye level are easiest.
species.identify: The new growth at branch tips in late spring: pale bright green, soft, still wearing a papery brown sheath.
species.use: Citrusy. Syrup, salt, shortbread, beer. A pinch goes a long way.
species.lookalikes: Yew is the one to know, and every part of it but the red flesh is toxic. Canada yew is a native forest shrub across the east and Pacific yew a native tree in BC. Spruce is easy: square needles that roll between your fingers. Fir is the trap, because fir needles are flat like yew's — so turn a fir needle over: fir has two white stripes underneath and smells of resin or citrus when crushed, and firs carry upright cones. Yew needles are plain green beneath with no white lines, have no resin smell, and the tree bears red berry-like cups instead of cones.

species.name: Cattail shoots
species.habitat: Marsh edges, ditches and pond margins in clean water.
species.identify: Tall, flat, strap-like leaves wrapping a round, spongy base, often beside last year's brown spikes; peel the inner shoot from the base for the white 'Cossack asparagus'.
species.use: Inner shoots raw or cooked; green flower spikes boiled like corn.
species.lookalikes: Before the flower spike appears, cattail leaves resemble yellow flag iris — iris is toxic. Iris leaves fan out flat from the base and the stem is flattened, with a vein down the centre; a cattail shoot is round and spongy. When in doubt, leave it.
species.caution: Cattails concentrate pollutants. Harvest only from clean water, never ditches beside roads or farm runoff.

species.name: Wild violets
species.habitat: Lawns, woodland edges, shaded banks.
species.identify: Heart-shaped leaves and five-petalled purple flowers, each on its own leafless stalk straight from the ground.
species.use: Flowers candied or in salad; young leaves mild and mucilaginous in soup.
species.lookalikes: Lesser celandine (fig buttercup) has similar heart-shaped leaves and is poisonous raw; it has shiny yellow buttercup flowers and grows in carpets from little tubers. Violets have purple (sometimes white) five-petalled flowers on leafless stalks. Avoid sprayed lawns.

species.name: Wild strawberry
species.habitat: Sunny meadows, old fields, forest edges and roadside banks.
species.identify: Three toothed leaflets, white five-petalled flowers, and a small red berry with seeds sitting in tiny pits on the surface.
species.use: Eat on the spot — they don't travel. Ten times the flavour of a supermarket berry.
species.lookalikes: Mock strawberry (Potentilla indica) has yellow flowers and a bland, upward-pointing berry. Harmless, just tasteless.

species.name: Serviceberry (saskatoon)
species.habitat: Coulees, forest edges, hedgerows and countless city plantings.
species.identify: A shrub or small tree with oval, toothed leaves; berries look like small blueberries but carry a tiny five-pointed crown at the tip and have soft seeds inside.
species.use: Pies, jam, pemmican. Sweeter and nuttier than blueberry.
species.lookalikes: Buckthorn berries are black and purgative; serviceberry keeps that little crown and grows on a shrub with smooth grey bark.

species.name: Mulberries
species.habitat: Old lots, alleys, park edges — one of the great urban foraging trees.
species.identify: Blackberry-shaped fruit growing on a tree, not a cane. Leaves vary wildly on one tree, from plain ovals to mitten shapes. Most wild mulberries are the introduced white mulberry, whose ripe fruit may be white, pink or black; the native red mulberry is rare in Canada.
species.use: Spread a sheet and shake the branch. Eat fresh, or bake — they're low in acid, so add lemon.
species.lookalikes: Few trees bear a fruit like it; make sure yours is a mulberry before you eat. Unripe green fruit and the milky sap can upset stomachs. Red mulberry is endangered in Canada — leave those trees be.

species.name: Elderflower
species.habitat: Damp roadsides, ditches, streambanks and field edges.
species.identify: Big flat-topped creamy flower heads on a woody, many-stemmed shrub with opposite compound leaves; young twigs are filled with soft white pith.
species.use: Cordial, fritters, sparkling wine. Snip the whole head, shake out the insects, never wash.
species.lookalikes: Water hemlock and poison hemlock also have white umbels — but they are herbaceous plants with hollow, often purple-blotched stems, not woody shrubs. Water hemlock is the deadliest plant on the continent.
species.caution: Learn the difference before you pick a white flower head. Elder is a shrub with bark.

species.name: Golden chanterelle
species.habitat: Mossy conifer and oak forest, usually a week after warm rain. Pacific Northwest and the Appalachians are the strongholds.
species.identify: Egg-yolk to apricot yellow, vase or trumpet shaped, with blunt forking false gills that run down the stem like melted wax. Smells of apricots.
species.use: Dry-sauté first to drive off water, then butter. Freezes well cooked.
species.lookalikes: Jack-o'-lantern (Omphalotus) grows in dense clusters on wood, has true knife-edge gills and glows faintly; it causes violent illness. Chanterelles grow singly from soil.

species.name: Wild raspberries
species.habitat: Sunny edges, old clearcuts, burns and fence lines.
species.identify: Compound berry that pulls free of its core, leaving a hollow thimble. Canes are prickly, leaves white-woolly underneath.
species.use: Fresh, jam, or frozen on a tray the day you pick.
species.lookalikes: Other brambles are the usual confusion, and their fruit is edible too. What matters is the berry: a raspberry pulls free leaving a hollow cup. Never eat an unknown red berry that is smooth and shiny instead of made of little beads.

species.name: Salmonberry
species.habitat: Wet coastal forest, stream edges and roadside thickets from Alaska to northwestern California.
species.identify: Tall arching canes with three leaflets, magenta flowers early, then a raspberry-shaped berry in salmon-orange to deep red.
species.use: Eat fresh; the flavour is mild and varies bush to bush — taste before you fill a bucket.
species.lookalikes: Other brambles are the usual confusion, and their fruit is edible too. Anything that is not a prickly, three-leaflet cane with a raspberry-like berry is not salmonberry.

species.name: Wild blueberries
species.habitat: Acidic, sandy or rocky barrens, burns, bog edges and open pine woods.
species.identify: Low shrubs with small oval leaves; berries dusty blue with a five-pointed crown at the tip and green-white flesh inside. In the east it is the lowbush blueberry (V. angustifolium) of barrens and burns; in the western mountains and on the coast, the oval-leaf and bog blueberries, taller and picked the same way.
species.use: Rake or hand-pick. Freeze on trays the same day.
species.lookalikes: The crown at the tip is the tell. Avoid any blue-black berry on a plant with opposite leaves or milky sap.

species.name: Huckleberries
species.habitat: Mid to high elevation mountain slopes, old burns and open conifer forest in the Rockies, Cascades and BC interior.
species.identify: Waist-high shrubs, thin oval leaves, single dark purple berries in the leaf axils — one per stem, not in clusters.
species.use: Pie, jam, pancakes. The best-flavoured berry in the mountain west.
species.lookalikes: Blueberries are close cousins and edible. Keep clear of any black or blue berry on a plant with different leaves — twisted-stalk, baneberry and nightshade all grow in mountain forest. Huckleberries hang singly under the leaves, with a small crown at the tip.
species.caution: Prime bear habitat in August. Carry spray and talk loudly.

species.name: Thimbleberry
species.habitat: Forest edges, roadcuts and clearings, often in big thickets.
species.identify: Large soft maple-shaped leaves, no thorns, white flowers, and a shallow, wide scarlet berry like a thimble that collapses when picked.
species.use: Eat immediately — they will not survive a walk home. Excellent jam if you can gather enough.
species.lookalikes: Other brambles are the usual confusion, and their fruit is edible. Thimbleberry is the thornless one with big soft maple-shaped leaves; don't eat any red berry from a plant you can't name.

species.name: Prickly pear (tunas & nopales)
species.habitat: Dry rocky slopes, desert flats and sandy prairie.
species.identify: Flat paddle cactus; the fruit (tuna) sits on the paddle rim and ripens deep magenta. Both fruit and young pads are used. Which prickly pear depends on where you are: Engelmann's in the desert Southwest (zones 8–11), the low plains and brittle prickly pears of the prairies and BC (hardy to zone 3), and the eastern prickly pear of sandy ground in the east (zones 5–9).
species.use: Tongs and a bucket. Burn or scrub off the glochids, then peel. Syrup, jelly, margaritas; pads grilled as nopales.
species.lookalikes: Other cacti share the spines but not the fruit shape; stick to the flat-padded Opuntia. The real hazard is the hair-fine glochids — thick gloves, and never rub your eyes.
species.caution: The tiny hair-like spines are the hazard, not the big ones.

set.identify: Flat paddle cactus; the fruit (tuna) sits on the paddle rim and ripens deep magenta. Both fruit and young pads are used.

species.name: Wild blackberries
species.habitat: Old fields, powerline cuts, forest edges — full sun and disturbed ground.
species.identify: Berry keeps its white core when picked (unlike raspberry). Thorny arching canes, five leaflets.
species.use: Ripe means dull black and falling into your hand; shiny black is still sour.
species.lookalikes: Other brambles (dewberries, black raspberries) are the usual confusion, and they are edible too. What matters is the berry: a blackberry keeps its white core. Avoid smooth, shiny black berries on plants without thorny canes.

species.name: Chicken of the woods
species.habitat: Shelves on standing or fallen hardwood, especially oak. Same tree fruits for years.
species.identify: Overlapping fan-shaped brackets, bright orange on top, sulphur-yellow underneath with tiny pores — never gills.
species.use: Only the tender outer edges. Cook thoroughly; texture genuinely like chicken.
species.lookalikes: Dyer's polypore, at the base of conifers, is velvety brown with yellow pores and is not one to eat. Reactions are reported more often from specimens on conifer or eucalyptus (and sometimes oak), and old tough ones upset stomachs. Take young, soft growth, cook it well, and try a little the first time.
species.caution: Try a small amount the first time — a minority of people react to it even when correctly identified.

species.name: Hen of the woods (maitake)
species.habitat: The base of old oaks, at the trunk or on stumps. Returns to the same tree each autumn.
species.identify: A big grey-brown rosette of overlapping spoon-shaped fronds on a branching white stem, with pores underneath.
species.use: One find can weigh several kilos. Roast, or dry the surplus.
species.lookalikes: Berkeley's polypore is similar but tougher and paler, and black-staining polypore bruises black; both grow at oak bases and are not dangerous. Check the underside for pores, never gills.

species.name: Giant puffball
species.habitat: Pastures, lawns, hedgerows and open woods — often a white ball visible from the road.
species.identify: Smooth white ball, football-sized or larger. Slice it top to bottom: it must be pure white and uniform like a marshmallow, with no gills, no outline of a mushroom, no yellowing.
species.use: Slice thick and fry like a cutlet. Only while pure white inside.
species.lookalikes: A button-stage Amanita — including the destroying angel — looks like a small white ball until you slice it and see the outline of a young mushroom. Always slice.
species.caution: Any yellow or olive inside means it is past it: discard.

species.name: King bolete (porcini)
species.habitat: Under conifers and oaks; spectacular flushes along the Pacific coast after the first autumn rains.
species.identify: Fat white stem with a fine raised net near the top, brown 'bun' cap, and a sponge of white-to-yellow pores that never stain blue.
species.use: Slice and dry — the flavour concentrates. Firm young buttons are the prize.
species.lookalikes: Bitter bolete (Tylopilus) has pink pores and ruins a dish; boletes with red pores or that stain dark blue should be left alone.

species.name: Lobster mushroom
species.habitat: Conifer and mixed forest, often half-buried in duff.
species.identify: Not a mushroom but a parasitic mould that turns its host bright orange-red and pimply, with firm white flesh inside. A strong fishy smell means it is old.
species.use: Firm and genuinely lobster-like. Scrub well, cook thoroughly.
species.lookalikes: The host is almost always an edible Russula or Lactarius. Take only firm, bright specimens — soft, blackening ones are old.

species.name: Matsutake (pine mushroom)
species.habitat: Sandy soil under pine, fir and tanoak; often pushing up a hump of needles.
species.identify: White to buff, dense and heavy, with a distinctive cinnamon-and-gym-socks smell you can identify blindfolded. Gills white, with a partial veil.
species.use: Highly prized in Japan; sliced thin in broth or rice.
species.lookalikes: Amanita smithiana grows in the same forests, is also white, and causes kidney failure. It has no matsutake smell and its base is bulbous with a fragile veil.
species.caution: If it does not smell strongly of spice and socks, leave it — and even if it does, dig up the whole stem and check the base for Smith's amanita's bulb before you eat it.

species.name: Oyster mushroom
species.habitat: Dead and dying hardwood — poplar, willow, beech, maple. Fruits after cool rain, often in winter.
species.identify: Shelving clusters of oyster-shaped caps with white gills that run down a stubby off-centre stem or none at all. Faint anise smell.
species.use: A good beginner mushroom once identified with certainty. Always cook it; roast hard so the edges crisp.
species.lookalikes: Angel wings (Pleurocybella porrigens) is thin, pure white and grows on conifer wood; it has been linked to deaths in people with kidney disease, so take oysters from hardwood only. Jack-o'-lantern is orange, with true gills, in clusters on stumps and buried roots. Little brown mushrooms with rings on the stem are never oysters.

species.name: Lion's mane
species.habitat: Wounds and broken limbs on living hardwoods, especially beech, oak and maple.
species.identify: A white pom-pom of soft downward-hanging spines, growing straight out of a tree trunk.
species.use: Tear into chunks, dry-sear, then butter. Tastes remarkably of crab.
species.lookalikes: Its own relatives — comb tooth and bear's head tooth — are the usual look-alikes, and they are edible. Check that yours is fresh and white, not yellowed.

species.name: Wild hazelnuts
species.habitat: Hedgerows, forest edges and fence lines.
species.identify: Multi-stemmed shrub; nuts in clusters. American hazelnut (east and prairies) wraps each nut in ragged leafy husks; beaked hazelnut (the north and west) hides it in a long, bristly tube — wear gloves.
species.use: Pick as husks turn tan — squirrels take them within days. Cure two weeks before cracking.
species.lookalikes: Witch-hazel has similar leaves but woody seed capsules, not nuts. Eat only nuts you found in a leafy or bristly hazel husk.

species.name: Black walnut
species.habitat: Old farmsteads, river bottoms, fence lines and city parks.
species.identify: Tennis-ball green husks lying under a tall tree with long compound leaves; the husk stains everything it touches brown.
species.use: Husk outdoors with gloves, wash, cure a month, then crack. Deep, wine-like flavour, unlike any store walnut.
species.lookalikes: Horse chestnut and buckeye nuts are toxic; they have spiny or smooth leathery husks that split open, not a solid green ball.
species.caution: The husk juice permanently stains skin, clothes and driveways.

set.lookalikes: Butternut is a close relative with football-shaped sticky husks; it is uncommon and declining, so leave butternuts on the tree. Horse chestnut and buckeye nuts are toxic; they have spiny or smooth leathery husks that split open, not a solid green ball.
