set.habitat: Old farmsteads, fence lines and city parks.

species.name: Pawpaw
species.habitat: Shady river bottoms and creek flats, in dense clonal patches under bigger trees.
species.identify: Understorey tree with huge drooping leaves and green mango-shaped fruit; ripe ones fall and give to a gentle squeeze.
species.use: The largest native fruit on the continent — custard texture, mango-banana flavour. Eat within days or freeze the pulp.
species.lookalikes: Few other eastern trees bear a big green fruit in the shade; check for the huge drooping leaves. Don't eat the skin or seeds.
species.caution: A minority of people react to pawpaw. Try a little the first time.

species.name: American persimmon
species.habitat: Old fields, fence lines and open woods.
species.identify: Blocky alligator-hide bark; orange fruit the size of a plum, only ripe when it is wrinkled, squishy and usually on the ground.
species.use: Pulp for pudding and bread. Wait for wrinkles — an unripe persimmon is astringent enough to make your mouth feel like felt.
species.lookalikes: The main danger is an unripe persimmon: astringent, and eaten in quantity it can form hard masses in the stomach. Wait for wrinkles.

species.name: Elderberries
species.habitat: Damp ditches, streambanks and field edges — the same shrubs that flowered in June.
species.identify: Flat, heavy clusters of tiny purple-black berries on red-tinged stems, on a shrub with opposite compound leaves.
species.use: Always cooked. Syrup, jelly, wine. Strip berries with a fork and discard every bit of green stem.
species.lookalikes: Red elderberry flowers earlier in egg- to pyramid-shaped clusters and has bright red berries; treat them as not edible — it is the common elder of the Pacific coast. Pokeweed berries hang in a grape-like spike from a thick purple stem and are toxic.
species.caution: Raw berries, leaves and stems contain cyanogenic compounds. Cook them.

species.name: Rose hips
species.habitat: Hedgerows, roadsides and old gardens.
species.identify: The red-orange fruit left after a wild rose blooms, topped with a dried five-pointed crown of sepals.
species.use: Best after the first frost. Halve, scrape out the seeds and irritant hairs, then dry for tea or cook into jelly.
species.lookalikes: Bittersweet nightshade has smooth, oval, shiny red berries in drooping clusters on a vine with purple star flowers, and is poisonous. Bittersweet vines (Celastrus) carry orange-red berries in yellow husks, and yew and bush honeysuckle also have red fruit. A rose hip grows on a thorny rose bush and keeps a dried crown of sepals at its tip.

species.name: Staghorn sumac
species.habitat: Roadsides, embankments and old fields, in colonies.
species.identify: Upright, fuzzy, deep-red cone-shaped clusters on velvety branches. Red and upright is the rule.
species.use: Steep in cold water for an hour for pink lemonade; dry and grind for the spice.
species.lookalikes: Poison sumac has drooping white-green berries and grows in swamps. Staghorn's are red, fuzzy and upright on velvety twigs; white, drooping berries mean poison sumac — leave it.
species.caution: Pick before heavy rain washes away the tart coating. Sumac is a cousin of cashew and mango — skip it if you're allergic to either.

set.lookalikes: Poison sumac, rare in Canada and found only in southern Ontario and Quebec (Natural Resources Canada), has drooping white-green berries and grows in swampy woods. Staghorn's are red, fuzzy and upright on velvety twigs; white, drooping berries mean poison sumac — leave it.

Poison sumac, the dangerous relative with drooping white-green berries, grows in Canada only in southern Ontario and Quebec (Natural Resources Canada). Staghorn's are red, fuzzy and upright on velvety twigs; white, drooping berries on any sumac-like shrub mean leave it.

species.name: Wild grapes
species.habitat: Riverbanks, fence lines and forest edges, climbing high into trees.
species.identify: Woody vine with shreddy bark and forked tendrils opposite the leaves; small purple-black grapes with seeds.
species.use: Very tart — jelly, juice, verjuice. The young leaves are the ones for dolmades.
species.lookalikes: Canada moonseed is the danger: it has no tendrils, its 'grapes' contain a single flat crescent seed, and it is toxic. Grapes have one to four egg-shaped seeds, never a crescent.

species.name: Highbush cranberry
species.habitat: Wet thickets, streambanks and forest edges.
species.identify: Maple-like three-lobed leaves and translucent scarlet berries in flat clusters, each with one flat stone.
species.use: Sour and musky raw; excellent jelly, better after frost.
species.lookalikes: European guelder rose looks nearly identical and is bitter. Red baneberry, a knee-high plant of the same woods, has glossy red berries on stalks and is highly toxic. Highbush cranberry is a tall shrub with maple-like leaves.

species.name: Wild cranberries
species.habitat: Sphagnum bogs and wet, acidic heathland.
species.identify: Thin trailing vines through the moss with tiny evergreen leaves; hard red berries sitting on top of the moss. The large cranberry (V. macrocarpon) is the one of eastern bogs; across the boreal north and the taiga it is the small cranberry (V. oxycoccos), pea-sized on even finer vines, picked the same way.
species.use: Sauce, drying, freezing. They keep for months in a cold room.
species.lookalikes: Winterberry holly grows in the same wet ground and has bright red berries on an upright shrub; they are mildly toxic. Cranberries trail through the moss on thread-thin vines with tiny evergreen leaves.

species.name: Chokecherry
species.habitat: Coulees, fence lines, forest edges and riverbanks.
species.identify: Long drooping clusters of dark red-to-black cherries on a small tree with finely toothed oval leaves.
species.use: Astringent raw; superb syrup and jelly once cooked and strained.
species.lookalikes: Common buckthorn has black berries in clusters along the stem, not in hanging chains, and they cause vomiting and diarrhea. Black cherry is a tall tree with similar edible fruit. The pits, leaves and stems of chokecherry itself contain cyanide compounds — never crush or eat the pits.
species.caution: Strain out every pit. Wilted leaves are poisonous to livestock.

species.name: Wild and abandoned apples
species.habitat: Old farmsteads, fence lines, roadsides — anywhere a farm once stood.
species.identify: An apple tree gone feral: small, spotty, often superb fruit. Every seedling tree is genetically unique.
species.use: Cider, sauce, jelly. Taste one from each tree; occasionally you find a great one worth grafting.
species.lookalikes: Crabapples look alike and are edible too, if very sour. Spit out the seeds: like cherry pits, they contain cyanide compounds.
species.caution: Ask before picking on private land; a hedgerow tree usually belongs to someone.

species.name: Acorns
species.habitat: Any oak — parks, streets, woodlots and savanna.
species.identify: Collect brown, freshly fallen nuts with no weevil holes; float them in water and discard the ones that swim.
species.use: Must be leached: grind, then rinse in repeated changes of water until the bitterness is gone. Flour for pancakes and bread. White oaks leach fastest.
species.lookalikes: Horse chestnut and buckeye nuts are highly toxic; they are big, glossy and brown with a pale scar, from a spiny or leathery husk — no scaly cap. An acorn always sits in a little scaly cup.
species.caution: Unleached acorns are astringent and hard on the stomach.

species.name: Wild pecans
species.habitat: River bottoms and old plantings through Texas, the lower Mississippi and the south.
species.identify: Tall tree with long compound leaves; thin-shelled nuts in husks that split into four neat sections.
species.use: Native seedling pecans are small but far richer than orchard varieties.
species.lookalikes: Bitternut hickory is inedibly bitter; its husk splits only partway and the nut is nearly round.

species.name: Shagbark hickory nuts
species.habitat: Mature hardwood forest and old fence lines.
species.identify: Unmistakable bark peeling off in long vertical shaggy plates; husks split cleanly into four to release a pale, sweet nut.
species.use: The best-flavoured wild nut in the east. Crack, pick, and use anywhere pecans go.
species.lookalikes: Bitternut hickory looks similar but the nut is bitter; shagbark's shaggy bark is the tell.

species.name: Hawthorn berries
species.habitat: Hedgerows, pasture edges and old fields.
species.identify: Thorny small tree with lobed leaves and clusters of small red haws, each holding one to five hard stones. Cut one open to see the stones.
species.use: Jelly, fruit leather, ketchup. Mild and apple-like.
species.lookalikes: Confirm the thorns and the stones inside before eating any red berry — cotoneaster, bittersweet nightshade and yew all carry red fruit. The flesh of the haw is the part to use: like apple and cherry seeds, the seeds are not eaten, so strain them out and never crush them.
species.caution: Hawthorn may raise digoxin levels and add to the effect of blood thinners; if you take heart medicines, ask a doctor first.

species.name: Wintergreen (teaberry)
species.habitat: Acidic soil under pine and oak, often with blueberry.
species.identify: Ankle-high evergreen with thick glossy oval leaves and a bright red berry; crush a leaf and it smells exactly of wintergreen.
species.use: Berries persist under snow — a winter trail nibble. Leaves make tea.
species.lookalikes: Partridgeberry is a harmless lookalike with paired leaves and two dimples on the fruit; the wintergreen smell settles it.
species.caution: Wintergreen contains methyl salicylate, an aspirin relative: the oil is toxic in quantity, and anyone allergic to aspirin or taking blood thinners should avoid it.

species.name: Salal
species.habitat: The dominant understorey shrub of coastal forest from Alaska to California.
species.identify: Leathery, glossy, egg-shaped leaves on a knee-to-shoulder-high shrub; hairy dark blue-black berries in a row along a reddish stalk.
species.use: Sweet and mealy; traditional dried cakes, good jam, excellent with the last of the huckleberries.
species.lookalikes: Other blue-black berries grow in coastal forest; salal's come in a row along a single reddish, hairy stalk under leathery egg-shaped leaves. If it isn't on that plant, don't eat it.

species.name: Sea grape
species.habitat: Beach dunes and coastal hammocks of central and south Florida. Shoreline plants are protected — look for landscape plantings instead.
species.identify: Big round leathery leaves with red veins; grape-like clusters that ripen unevenly to purple.
species.use: Pick only the purple ones. Jelly and wine.
species.lookalikes: Manchineel is the danger: a highly toxic beach tree of south Florida with small green apple-like fruit and pointed oval leaves; even its sap and rainwater dripping from it burn skin. Sea-grape has big round leaves and fruit in hanging grape-like bunches.

species.name: Beach plum
species.habitat: Coastal dunes and sandy scrub from the Maritimes to Virginia.
species.identify: Low sprawling shrub in the sand, with dusty purple plums about the size of a marble.
species.use: Legendary jelly. Tart and rich.
species.lookalikes: Other wild plums and cherries grow near the coast and have edible flesh too. Like all of them, beach plum's pits and leaves contain cyanide compounds — spit out the stones and never crush them.

species.name: Juniper berries
species.habitat: Dry rocky slopes, barrens and open woods.
species.identify: Low spiky evergreen with needles in whorls of three, each with a white stripe on top; the 'berries' are fleshy blue cones that take two, sometimes three, years to ripen — so green and blue ones hang together.
species.use: Dry and use for game, sauerkraut and gin-style flavouring. A few go a long way.
species.lookalikes: Common juniper is the one to use. Avoid ornamental junipers and any yew — flat needles, red fleshy cups, toxic.
species.caution: Not for use in pregnancy or kidney disease, or in large amounts.

species.name: Chaga
species.habitat: Living birch trees in cold northern forest — easiest to spot with the leaves down.
species.identify: A black, cracked, charcoal-like mass bursting out of a birch trunk, rusty orange-brown and corky inside.
species.use: Chunks simmered for tea. Take only part of a conk, leave the rest, and never take from a dead tree.
species.lookalikes: Burls and old black knots are woody through; chaga's orange interior is the tell.
species.caution: Slow-growing and now heavily over-harvested. Take sparingly, and never from a small tree. Chaga is very high in oxalate (heavy daily use has damaged kidneys) and may thin the blood.

species.name: Miner's lettuce
species.habitat: Shaded, damp ground in the winter-wet west — banks, oak understorey, north-facing slopes.
species.identify: Distinctive once mature: a round disc of leaf with the flower stalk coming up through the middle of it.
species.use: Raw salad green, mild and succulent. The best winter green on the west coast.
species.lookalikes: The round leaf with the flower stalk through the middle is the tell; young plants with only long-stalked leaves are harder to recognize, so wait for the disc. Like spinach it holds some oxalate, so eat it as a salad green, not by the bowlful.

species.name: Wild fennel
species.habitat: Roadsides, vacant lots and coastal scrub through California and the Pacific coast.
species.identify: Tall feathery blue-green plant with an unmistakable anise smell, a smooth green stem and yellow umbels.
species.use: Fronds, pollen and seeds. The pollen is a prized, pricey spice.
species.lookalikes: Poison hemlock grows in the same lots, has white flowers, purple-blotched stems, ferny leaves and a foul musty smell. Both stems can be hollow, so don't rely on that: yellow flowers and the smell of liquorice mean fennel; white flowers and blotches mean walk away. Hemlock kills.
species.caution: Smell it. Every time. If it does not smell strongly of anise, walk away.

set.habitat: Roadsides, vacant lots and coastal scrub.

species.name: Broadleaf plantain
species.habitat: Lawns, paths, driveways and trampled ground — it thrives on exactly the compacted soil nothing else likes.
species.identify: A flat rosette of broad oval leaves with five or more deep parallel veins running end to end, and a narrow greenish flower spike. Tear a leaf slowly and the veins pull out as tough strings.
species.use: Very young leaves cooked as a green; older ones are stringy. Better known as the field poultice for stings and scrapes.
species.lookalikes: Ribwort plantain is narrower-leaved and used the same way. Young foxglove rosettes are superficially similar and very poisonous — foxglove leaves are soft, downy and net-veined, never parallel-veined and stringy.
species.caution: Do not pick from lawns that may be treated, from roadsides, or from anywhere dogs are walked.

species.name: Yarrow
species.habitat: Meadows, road verges, old fields and dry open ground right across the continent.
species.identify: Soft, flat, very finely divided ferny leaves — the species name means a thousand leaves — a solid hairy stem, flat-topped clusters of small white or pink flowers, and a strong sharp aroma when crushed.
species.use: A bitter herb used sparingly; mostly gathered for tea and as the traditional wound herb rather than as food.
species.lookalikes: Poison hemlock and water hemlock have similarly feathery foliage and are lethal. Their stems are smooth and hollow, often purple-blotched, and they smell rank rather than aromatic. Yarrow's leaves are flat and soft and its stem is solid and hairy. If there is any doubt at all, walk away.
species.caution: In the daisy family, a common allergen, and it can irritate skin. Avoid in pregnancy.

species.name: Sheep sorrel
species.habitat: Poor, acidic, disturbed soil — fields, trails, gravel.
species.identify: Small arrow-shaped leaves with two backward-pointing lobes at the base, on a wiry reddish stem. Sharply lemony taste.
species.use: A tart accent in salads and sauces, not a bulk green.
species.lookalikes: Other docks have larger leaves without the two back-pointing lobes. The arrowhead leaf and sour taste are distinctive.
species.caution: High in oxalic acid — a garnish, not a plateful.

species.name: Lamb's quarters
species.habitat: Gardens, field edges and any freshly turned soil — one of the commonest weeds on the continent.
species.identify: Goosefoot-shaped leaves with a mealy white bloom on the undersides that beads water; ridged stems, often red-streaked.
species.use: Better than spinach, cooked the same way. Seeds are a quinoa relative.
species.lookalikes: Take a moment to distinguish from young nightshade — nightshade leaves lack the white mealy coating and the plant later carries green or black berries.

species.name: Purslane
species.habitat: Sidewalk cracks, garden beds and hot dry ground.
species.identify: Prostrate mats of smooth red stems with fat, glossy, paddle-shaped succulent leaves. No hairs, no milky sap.
species.use: Crunchy, lemony, high in omega-3. Raw in salad or stirred into soup at the end.
species.lookalikes: Prostrate spurge grows in the same cracks, has thin hairy leaves and milky sap, and is toxic. Purslane's sap is clear and its leaves are thick.

species.name: Burdock root
species.habitat: Waste ground, ditches and old barnyards.
species.identify: Dig first-year plants — a rosette of huge rhubarb-like leaves, woolly and pale underneath, with no flower stalk yet.
species.use: Great burdock (A. lappa) is the gobo of Japanese cooking, and common burdock's root is used the same way. Long taproot, deep digging; scrub, slice and braise.
species.lookalikes: Second-year plants have the burs and a woody, useless root. Young rosettes can be confused with rhubarb (toxic leaves), foxglove, and cocklebur, whose seedlings are poisonous. Common burdock has hollow leaf stalks; great burdock's are solid and grooved. Only buy burdock root from a trusted source: bought 'burdock' tea has been found contaminated with belladonna.

species.name: Maple sap
species.habitat: Sugar bush, hedgerows and yards — any mature maple over 25 cm across.
species.identify: Sugar maple has five-lobed leaves with smooth-sided notches and grey furrowed bark. Any maple can be tapped; sugar and black maples run sweetest.
species.use: Tap when days rise above freezing and nights fall below. Roughly 40 litres of sap to one of syrup.
species.lookalikes: Birch and walnut can also be tapped, later and with different flavour. Tap only trees you can identify in winter from the bark and opposite buds.

species.name: Wood sorrel
species.habitat: Lawns, gardens, woodland edges and pavement cracks.
species.identify: Three heart-shaped leaflets that fold down at night, small yellow five-petalled flowers, and a sharp lemon taste.
species.use: A bright sour garnish; children love it. Small amounts.
species.lookalikes: Clover has oval leaflets with a pale chevron and tastes of nothing. Wood sorrel's heart-shaped leaflets fold down at night.
species.caution: Oxalic acid again — a nibble, not a salad bowl.

species.name: Chickweed
species.habitat: Garden beds, damp lawns and field edges — greenest in the cool months.
species.identify: Sprawling mats with small opposite oval leaves and a single line of fine hairs running up one side of the stem, switching sides at each leaf pair. Stretch the stem: an elastic inner core.
species.use: Mild raw green, best in winter salads and pesto.
species.lookalikes: Scarlet pimpernel is toxic and grows alongside; it has orange-red flowers, leaves without stalks and no line of hairs up the stem. Chickweed has tiny white star flowers and its single line of hairs.

species.name: Dulse
species.habitat: Cold Atlantic and Pacific shores, on rocks in the lower intertidal at low tide.
species.identify: Flat, hand-shaped, deep red-purple fronds with no midrib, attached by a small disc.
species.use: Cut above the holdfast so it regrows. Dry in sun; eat as chips or crumble into chowder.
species.lookalikes: Few dangerous seaweeds, but never harvest near outfalls or marinas.
species.caution: Check local closures and licence rules — several provinces and states regulate seaweed harvest.

species.name: Wild rice
species.habitat: Shallow, slow lakes and rivers of the upper Midwest and Ontario.
species.identify: Tall grass standing above the water with a branching seed head; grain is long, dark and slips free when ripe.
species.use: Harvested from a canoe with knocking sticks, then parched and winnowed.
species.lookalikes: Other tall marsh grasses carry no grain worth eating. The one danger is ergot: throw away any grain with pink or purplish blotches, or replaced by a hard, swollen growth.
species.caution: Culturally and legally protected. In Minnesota, Wisconsin and Ontario, ricing is regulated and reserved in many waters for Indigenous harvesters — check before you go.

species.name: Garlic mustard
species.habitat: Shaded and half-shaded ground: woodland edges, trail sides, floodplain forest, fence lines and the back of the yard, usually in dense carpets.
species.identify: Crush a leaf — it smells of garlic, and nothing that resembles it does. First-year rosettes have kidney-shaped, scallop-edged leaves; second-year stalks 30–100 cm (1–3 ft) carry triangular toothed leaves, small four-petalled white flowers and thin upright seed pods, over a white S-curved taproot.
species.use: Young leaves, flower buds and tender stalks, raw in small amounts or chopped and cooked: pesto, sautés, soup. Chop and let it sit a few minutes, or cook it, to drive off the cyanide-releasing compounds. Pull the whole plant, root and all — it is one of the worst woodland invaders on the continent, so take as much as you like and bag any flowering stalks.
species.lookalikes: Violets, ground ivy (creeping Charlie), henbit and young nettle all share the rounded or heart-shaped leaf of a first-year rosette. None smells of garlic. Ground ivy and henbit have square stems and opposite leaves; violet leaves come to a point with finer teeth; nettle stings.
species.caution: Raw garlic mustard contains cyanide precursors, so eat it raw only in small amounts and only occasionally. Pulled plants can still set seed — bag flowering stalks for the trash rather than composting them. Restricted or prohibited as a noxious weed in several states and provinces, which means do not move or plant it, not that you cannot pick it.

species.name: Red clover
species.habitat: Fields, roadsides, lawns, old pastures and sunny waste ground, from sea level to mountain meadows.
species.identify: Three oval leaflets each marked with a pale chevron, on hairy stems; round pink-purple flower heads 2–3 cm (about 1 in) across, each made of dozens of tiny pea flowers, sitting right above a pair of leaves.
species.use: Fresh flower heads, pulled apart over salads, steeped for tea or dried; young leaves cooked briefly. Pick heads that are fully pink and springy, never brown ones, and leave plenty for the bumblebees.
species.lookalikes: Crown vetch grows in the same road cuts with pink clover-like heads, but its leaves are ladders of 11 or more small paired leaflets, not three; it is not a food plant. White clover and alsike clover are eaten the same way. True vetches have tendrils and flowers in loose spikes.
species.caution: Tradition and herbal references advise against red clover in pregnancy, while breastfeeding, and alongside blood-thinning medication because of its isoflavones. Flowers are filling and not easily digested in quantity — a garnish or a tea, not a plateful. Avoid sprayed lawns and busy roadsides.

species.name: Chicory
species.habitat: Road shoulders, gravel lots, railway edges, pastures and hard-packed waste ground in full sun, often where nothing else is growing.
species.identify: Sky-blue flowers 3–4 cm (1–1½ in) across with square-ended, fringed petals, opening in the morning and closing by early afternoon, scattered up a stiff, nearly leafless, zigzag stem to 1.5 m (5 ft). A dandelion-like basal rosette with a bitter milky sap and a deep taproot.
species.use: Roots dug in autumn or early spring, scrubbed, chopped, roasted dark and ground for the classic coffee stretcher; young spring rosette leaves as a bitter salad or cooked green. Dig only where you may, and take the biggest roots from the thickest stands.
species.lookalikes: Before it flowers the rosette passes for dandelion or wild lettuce; all three are bitter and none is dangerous, and chicory’s leaves are rough-hairy underneath with a reddish midrib. Once the blue flowers open on a branched stem there is nothing else like it.
species.caution: Roadside chicory grows on exactly the soil that takes up road salt, exhaust metals and herbicide — dig roots well back from traffic. In the daisy family, so people allergic to ragweed or chamomile may react. Listed as a noxious weed in Colorado.

species.name: Wild bergamot (bee balm)
species.habitat: Dry sunny prairie, old fields, limestone road cuts, open oak woods and the edges of trails, often in big lavender drifts in July.
species.identify: Square hairy stem 60–120 cm (2–4 ft) with opposite, toothed, lance-shaped leaves that smell strongly of oregano and thyme when rubbed, topped by a single shaggy round head of lavender-pink tubular flowers above a ring of pale bracts.
species.use: Leaves and flowers, fresh or dried, as tea or as an oregano-like seasoning in anything savoury; the flowers pulled apart over salads. Take a few leaves from many plants, never the flower heads from a small patch — bumblebees and hummingbird moths depend on them.
species.lookalikes: Other mints share the square stem and opposite leaves, and none of the common ones is dangerous. Scarlet bee balm (Monarda didyma) is the garden and streamside cousin with red flowers and red-tinged bracts; it is used the same way. Spotted bee balm has yellow spotted flowers stacked in tiers above pink bracts.
species.caution: Strongly aromatic — it carries the same oils that flavour oregano and thyme, so it is a seasoning or a tea, not a bulk green. A medicine plant to many Plains and Great Lakes nations; pick lightly and never from a reserve, park or restoration planting.

species.name: Ground ivy (creeping Charlie)
species.habitat: Shady lawns, the damp side of the house, under hedges and along woodland paths, creeping in mats over anything moist and half-shaded.
species.identify: Trailing square stems that root at every node; opposite, round-to-kidney-shaped leaves with scalloped edges on long stalks; small blue-violet two-lipped flowers in the leaf axils in spring; and a sharp minty-skunky smell when crushed.
species.use: Young spring leaves and flowering tops, a few at a time: a bitter aromatic pot-herb for soup and stuffing, or dried for tea. It was the English bittering herb for ale before hops. A seasoning quantity, not a salad bowl.
species.lookalikes: Henbit and purple dead-nettle (both edible) are upright with leaves clasping the stem; common mallow has round stems and no smell; garlic mustard rosettes smell of garlic and have alternate leaves on round stems. Only ground ivy creeps with square stems and a mint smell.
species.caution: Poisonous to horses in quantity — keep it out of hay and paddocks. For people it contains volatile oils, so eat small amounts and leave it alone in pregnancy. Pick away from sprayed lawns and dog walks.

species.name: Selfheal (heal-all)
species.habitat: Lawns, trail edges, streamsides and open woods — low and sprawling where it is mown, upright to 30 cm (1 ft) where it is not.
species.identify: Square stem with opposite, oval to lance-shaped leaves that are barely toothed; and a stubby club-shaped flower head made of overlapping fringed bracts, with purple hooded flowers poking out a few at a time. The head stays on as a brown bristly knob long after flowering.
species.use: Leaves and flowering tops, raw in salads when young, cooked as a mild pot-herb, or dried for a tea in the European and Chinese herbal traditions. Cut the tops and leave the roots; it recovers quickly.
species.lookalikes: Bugleweed (Ajuga), the garden ground cover, has glossy often bronze leaves and flowers in whorls up a leafy spike rather than one compact bracted head; it is not a food plant. Other small mints have the square stem but not the knobby head.
species.caution: No known toxicity, but it is a lawn plant: avoid treated turf, dog runs and road edges. Pick lightly in places where it is a native wildflower rather than a weed.

species.name: Wild mint (Canada mint)
species.habitat: Wet feet: lakeshores, riverbanks, beaver meadows, ditches and the damp edge of a field, often smelled before it is seen.
species.identify: A square, usually hairy stem 20–60 cm (8–24 in) tall with opposite, toothed leaves and a strong, clean mint smell; the small pink-to-white flowers sit in tight whorls in the leaf axils up the stem, never in a spike at the top. If the flowers crown the stem, it is a different mint.
species.use: Leaves and flowering tops, fresh or dried, for tea, sauces, jelly and anywhere a garden mint goes. Pinch the tops and leave the runners; a patch regrows within weeks.
species.lookalikes: American pennyroyal and European pennyroyal also put their flowers in the leaf axils and smell minty, but pennyroyal is a slender plant under 40 cm (16 in) with small, nearly toothless leaves and a harsher, more pungent smell, and its oil is dangerously toxic — avoid pennyroyal in pregnancy altogether. Bugleweed and water horehound (Lycopus) grow in the same wet ground with the same axillary flower whorls, but they have no mint smell and white flowers.
species.caution: Mint and wet ground go together, so pick above the waterline and away from farm runoff and sewage outfalls. Strongly flavoured; a tea or seasoning, not a bulk green.

species.name: Goldenrod (Canada goldenrod)
species.habitat: Old fields, ditches, road edges, railway banks and clearings in full sun, in dense colonies that turn whole fields yellow in late summer.
species.identify: Stiff unbranched stems 1–1.5 m (3–5 ft) packed with alternate, lance-shaped, three-veined, toothed leaves and no basal rosette at flowering; a pyramidal plume of hundreds of tiny yellow flowers along the upper sides of arching branches. Insect-pollinated — its pollen is heavy and sticky and does not blow.
species.use: Flowering tops, fresh or dried, for a mild honey-and-hay flavoured tea; young leaves in spring as a cooked green; flowers in fritters and vinegar. Snip the top third of a few stems from a big stand.
species.lookalikes: Ragweed, which blooms at the same time and causes the hay fever goldenrod is blamed for, has green, inconspicuous flower spikes and deeply divided ferny leaves. Tansy ragwort and other ragworts and groundsels (Senecio, Jacobaea) carry yellow daisy-like flowers with distinct petals over ragged lobed leaves, and they contain liver-damaging pyrrolizidine alkaloids — goldenrod flowers are tiny and petal-less to the eye, and its leaves are simple and lance-shaped.
species.caution: In the daisy family: anyone allergic to ragweed, chamomile or chrysanthemums can react. Keep it to a tea. Do not confuse it with ragwort, whose alkaloids accumulate in the liver.

species.name: Pineapple weed (wild chamomile)
species.habitat: Trampled, compacted ground: gravel driveways, the edge of the ball diamond, farm gateways, sidewalk cracks and the middle of dirt roads.
species.identify: A low, hairless, ferny-leaved plant 5–30 cm (2–12 in) tall with cone-shaped yellow-green flower heads that have no petals at all. Crush a head: it smells unmistakably of pineapple. No pineapple smell, no pineapple weed.
species.use: Flower heads, fresh or dried, for a chamomile-like tea, in lemonade and syrup, or scattered over fruit. Pinch heads from many plants; they keep coming all summer.
species.lookalikes: Stinking chamomile (mayweed, Anthemis cotula) and scentless chamomile grow on the same ground with the same ferny leaves, but both carry white petals around a yellow centre, and mayweed smells foul and can blister skin. Pineapple weed never has petals and always smells of pineapple.
species.caution: Daisy family, so a chamomile or ragweed allergy is a reason to try a sip first. It grows where cars park and dogs stop — pick off the path and away from oil stains.

species.name: Common mallow (cheeseweed)
species.habitat: Gardens, barnyards, gravel lots, the base of walls and the edges of lawns, sprawling flat over bare, often dry, nitrogen-rich ground.
species.identify: Round, softly hairy, scalloped leaves with five to seven shallow lobes and a deep notch where the long stalk joins, on sprawling round stems from a tough taproot; small white-to-pale-pink five-petalled flowers with notched petals; and a flat fruit like a tiny wheel of cheese, split into a ring of wedge-shaped segments.
species.use: Young leaves raw or cooked — mild and mucilaginous, good for thickening soup; the green 'cheeses' nibbled raw or pickled; the mature seeds cooked like a grain. Cut leaves and cheeses and leave the taproot.
species.lookalikes: Ground ivy has similar round scalloped leaves but square stems, opposite leaves and a mint smell. Creeping buttercup has glossy, deeply cut, three-part leaves and an acrid sap that blisters the mouth raw. Young garden geranium (Geranium) seedlings have more deeply cut leaves and a long beaked fruit, never a cheese wheel.
species.caution: Mallow concentrates nitrates from rich soil, which has poisoned livestock; for people that means picking from lean ground rather than the manure pile or a heavily fertilised bed. Avoid sprayed and road-salted spots.

species.name: Wild carrot (Queen Anne's lace)
species.habitat: Dry roadsides, old fields, railway edges and waste ground in full sun — an introduced European biennial that is now a weed across most of the continent.
species.identify: A hairy, ribbed stem and leaves that smell exactly like carrot when crushed — both are required. In flower, a flat white umbel with a whorl of forked green bracts underneath and usually one dark purple floret in the centre; the old head curls into a bird’s nest.
species.use: The thin white taproot of first-year rosettes (no flower stalk yet), dug in fall or early spring and cooked like a woody carrot. Flowers can be dipped in batter. Dig only plants you have checked for hairs and smell, one at a time.
species.lookalikes: Poison hemlock and water hemlock can kill, and both are smooth-stemmed: poison hemlock is 1.5–3 m (5–10 ft) tall with a hairless, waxy, purple-blotched stem and a musty, mouse-like smell; water hemlock grows in wet ground with a purple-streaked stem and a chambered root that oozes yellow oily sap. Wild carrot is hairy, smells of carrot, and has the bracts under the umbel. No hairs, no carrot smell — walk away.
species.caution: People die from hemlocks mistaken for wild carrot or wild parsnip. First-year rosettes are the harvest, and they have no flowers to help you, so rely on the hairy leaf stalks and the carrot smell every single time. The sap can cause a mild rash in sunlight.

species.name: Cow parsnip
species.habitat: Moist meadows, streambanks, ditches, avalanche tracks and open woods from the coast to the subalpine; native across Canada and most of the US outside the Deep South.
species.identify: A huge native umbel plant, 1–3 m (3–10 ft), with a hollow, deeply ridged stem covered in soft hairs and no purple blotches; the leaves are enormous, three-parted and maple-like, up to 50 cm (20 in) across. Flat white flower heads 15–30 cm (6–12 in) wide in May–July.
species.use: Young leaf stalks and flower-bud stalks picked before the flowers open, peeled of every bit of outer skin, then eaten raw like celery or cooked. A long-standing Indigenous food across the Northwest, where it is called Indian celery. Wear gloves and long sleeves to pick and peel it.
species.lookalikes: Giant hogweed is the dangerous twin: 3–5 m (10–16 ft), a stem 5–10 cm (2–4 in) thick with purple blotches and coarse white bristles, leaves to 1.5 m (5 ft) across, and sap that causes severe blistering burns. Water hemlock and poison hemlock share its ground and are deadly — both are hairless, with finely divided leaves rather than huge maple-like ones, and purple-streaked or blotched stems.
species.caution: The sap causes phytophotodermatitis: on skin exposed to sunlight it raises painful blisters within 24–48 hours and dark marks that last months. Keep sap off skin and out of eyes, wash immediately, and stay out of the sun for two days after contact. Not a plant for children to handle.

species.name: Common milkweed
species.habitat: Old fields, roadsides, fencerows, railway banks and prairie edges in full sun, spreading into big colonies by underground runners.
species.identify: A single thick, unbranched, downy stem 0.6–1.5 m (2–5 ft) tall with big opposite oval leaves, velvety underneath, and milky sap. Round, fragrant pink-mauve flower balls in June–July, then fat, warty, spindle-shaped pods.
species.use: Only cooked. Young shoots under 20 cm (8 in), the unopened flower-bud clusters, and firm young pods under 4 cm (1.5 in), boiled until tender in water you throw away. Take a few shoots from a large colony and leave any plant carrying monarch eggs or caterpillars.
species.lookalikes: Dogbane (Apocynum cannabinum) also bleeds milky sap, so sap proves nothing. Dogbane is branched, with slender, smooth, reddish stems, small hairless opposite leaves and long thin pods in pairs; common milkweed is one thick, fuzzy, unbranched stem with big soft leaves and fat warty pods. Young pokeweed shoots have no milky sap and a smooth red-purple stem — pokeweed is poisonous and is never eaten.
species.caution: Raw milkweed contains cardiac glycosides that can affect the heart; poison centres advise against eating it at all, and the long tradition of eating it rests on boiling and discarding the water. If it tastes bitter, spit it out: it is dogbane, another milkweed, or one of the bitter strains of common milkweed found in parts of the Northeast — none of them should be eaten. Keep the sap out of eyes. Toxic to dogs, cats and horses.

species.name: Jerusalem artichoke (sunchoke)
species.habitat: Moist rich ground along rivers, ditches, fencerows and the edges of old fields and gardens, in dense colonies.
species.identify: A rough, hairy sunflower 1.5–3 m (5–10 ft) tall with broad, sandpapery leaves on winged stalks, and flowers 5–9 cm (2–3.5 in) across with 10–20 narrow yellow rays around a yellow-green centre in August–October. Dig to confirm: knobbly tubers on short runners under the clump.
species.use: The tubers, dug after the tops have died back in frost, through to early spring. Scrub, then roast, boil or slice raw into salads. Leave the small ones and every stand regrows.
species.lookalikes: Other tall sunflowers — sawtooth sunflower (smooth, waxy stem), giant sunflower (hairy stem but narrow, almost stalkless leaves) and woodland sunflowers — look alike above ground but make no fat tubers. None is dangerous; the tubers themselves are the identification.
species.caution: The inulin in the tubers ferments in the gut and gives many people wind and cramps — start with a small helping, especially for children. Never plant it loose in a garden: every fragment regrows.

species.name: Wapato (arrowhead)
species.habitat: Shallow still or slow water and mud — marsh edges, pond margins, sloughs, river backwaters and ditches — across the continent.
species.identify: Arrow-shaped leaves with two long basal lobes pointing backward and veins that radiate from where the stalk joins the blade; white three-petalled flowers in whorls of three on a separate leafless stalk, July–September. The tubers sit at the ends of long runners in the mud, up to 1 m (3 ft) from the plant.
species.use: Tubers dug or trodden loose in fall once the leaves yellow — the traditional way is to wade in and work them free with your feet so they float. Always cooked: roasted, boiled or baked like a small potato with a chestnut note. A culturally important Indigenous food; take little, from big stands, and never from a bed someone else tends.
species.lookalikes: Arrow arum (Peltandra virginica) grows in the same mud with a similar arrow-shaped leaf, but it has one strong midvein with side veins running out to the edge, a green hooded spathe instead of white flowers, and a drooping cluster of green-brown berries; its root and berries are loaded with calcium oxalate and burn the mouth. Pickerelweed has heart-shaped leaves with many fine parallel veins and a blue-violet flower spike.
species.caution: Wapato is a sacred and historic staple of the Katzie and other Coast Salish peoples of the lower Fraser and of the Chinookan peoples of the lower Columbia, and communities are restoring their beds — respect them. Many wetlands are inside parks, refuges and conservation areas where digging is prohibited; check first and harvest only from clean water.

species.name: Groundnut (hopniss)
species.habitat: Moist thickets, riverbanks, lakeshores and the brushy edges of wetlands, twining up shrubs and tall herbs.
species.identify: A twining herbaceous vine with milky sap — unusual in a pea — and leaves of 5–7 oval, pointed leaflets; dense clusters of fragrant maroon-brown pea flowers in July–September. Follow the thin root and you find tubers strung along it like beads on a cord.
species.use: Tubers 1–5 cm (0.5–2 in) across, dug from fall after frost through early spring, scrubbed and boiled 20–30 minutes, then fried or roasted. Nutty, potato-like and high in protein. Replant the smallest beads where you dug.
species.lookalikes: Hog peanut (Amphicarpaea bracteata) climbs the same thickets but has only three leaflets per leaf, pale pink flowers and no chain of tubers. Wild yam (Dioscorea villosa) has heart-shaped single leaves and is not a pea. Neither is dangerous; the beaded tubers on a milky-sapped pea vine are the identification.
species.caution: A small share of people react to groundnut with vomiting, cramps and diarrhoea, often not on the first meal but on a later one. Eat a small portion the first several times, cook it thoroughly, and stop at any sign of trouble.

species.name: Evening primrose
species.habitat: Dry, open, disturbed ground — roadsides, railway banks, gravel pits, dunes, old fields and garden edges — in full sun.
species.identify: A first-year rosette of long, narrow, slightly hairy leaves, each with a prominent white or pink midrib and often red flecks; the second-year stalk is 1–2 m (3–6 ft), reddish and hairy, with four-petalled yellow flowers that open at dusk and a cross-shaped stigma.
species.use: The pink-red taproot of first-year rosettes, dug in fall or very early spring and boiled in a change of water — peppery and parsnip-like. Young leaves and shoots cooked, flower buds and flowers, and the tiny seeds. Leave some rosettes to flower.
species.lookalikes: Mullein rosettes are thick and woolly like felt; curly dock is hairless with crisped, wavy edges and no white midrib. Foxglove, naturalized in the Pacific Northwest and common in gardens, also makes a rosette: its leaves are soft, wrinkled and woolly underneath with no white midrib, and every part is deadly.
species.caution: Raw, the root and shoots sting the throat, and a few people find them irritating even cooked — taste a little first. Only first-year plants are worth digging.

species.name: Watercress
species.habitat: Cold, clear, flowing water — spring runs, limestone creeks, seeps and the heads of streams — where it builds floating mats; introduced from Europe and now across most of the continent.
species.identify: Hollow, hairless stems that float or sprawl and root at every node; pinnate leaves with 3–9 rounded leaflets, the end one largest; small white four-petalled flowers in April–July; and a clean mustard-pepper taste.
species.use: Cut the leafy tops above the waterline with scissors, in spring and again in fall. Cook it — soup, steamed, stir-fried — unless it comes from water you would happily drink. Or root a sprig in a pot and grow your own.
species.lookalikes: Water hemlock can grow on the same banks and through the same mats and is deadly: narrow, sharply toothed leaflets with veins ending in the notches, an upright purple-streaked stem, a chambered root — and no mustard taste, but never taste-test it. Water parsnip and other wet-ground carrot relatives have narrow toothed leaflets and a carroty smell. Marsh yellowcress has yellow flowers and stands up on mud.
species.caution: The danger is the water, not the plant. Watercress downstream of cattle or sheep can carry liver-fluke cysts, and any untreated water can carry Giardia and bacteria; washing does not reliably remove them, cooking does. Avoid streams below farms, pastures and roads.

set.habitat: Cold, clear, flowing water — spring runs, limestone creeks, seeps and the heads of streams — where it builds floating mats.

species.name: Wild sarsaparilla
species.habitat: Dry to moist woods — under pine, aspen, maple and spruce — where it carpets the floor in large colonies 20–50 cm (8–20 in) tall.
species.identify: One leaf stalk rising from the ground and splitting into three branches, each with 3–5 finely toothed oval leaflets, so it looks like three leaves on one stem; a separate, shorter, leafless stalk underneath carries usually three round clusters of greenish-white flowers in May–June, then blue-black berries.
species.use: The long, aromatic horizontal rhizome, traditionally simmered for a root-beer-flavoured drink or tea. Dig a short length from a big colony, wash, chop and simmer; leave the rest to regrow. The berries are not eaten.
species.lookalikes: Poison ivy seedlings share the spring woods: each poison ivy leaf has three leaflets with coarse, irregular teeth or lobes, and the plant climbs or sprawls; sarsaparilla’s single stalk splits into three branches of 3–5 finely serrated leaflets and never climbs. Spikenard (Aralia racemosa) is a taller leafy plant with berries in a long plume; bristly sarsaparilla has a bristly woody base. Neither is dangerous.
species.caution: The berries are reported to make people ill and are left for the birds. Do not confuse the rhizome with American ginseng, which grows in the same rich woods and is protected across its range.

species.name: Sochan (cutleaf coneflower)
species.habitat: Moist bottomland woods, streambanks, wet meadows and ditches, in sun or part shade, often in big stands.
species.identify: Basal leaves deeply cut into 3–7 lobes like a turkey’s foot, on a smooth, hairless stem with a waxy blue-green bloom, 1–3 m (3–10 ft) tall. July–September flowers have 6–12 drooping yellow rays around a green cone that yellows as it ages.
species.use: The spring leaves and tender shoots, and a second flush of basal leaves in fall, blanched and then fried or sautéed — a Cherokee traditional green with a celery-like taste. Pick leaves, never the root, and leave most of every clump.
species.lookalikes: Other coneflowers have hairy stems and dark brown or black cones — black-eyed Susan and gray-headed coneflower — and are not eaten. Buttercups in the same wet meadows have glossy, lobed leaves and are acrid and toxic raw. Learn sochan in flower before you pick the rosettes in spring.
species.caution: Cook it; the foliage has poisoned pigs, sheep and horses that grazed it in quantity. In western mountain meadows, monkshood and larkspur grow in the same wet ground with deeply cut leaves and are deadly — never pick a cut-leaved rosette there you have not watched flower.

species.name: Beechnuts
species.habitat: Rich, well-drained hardwood slopes with sugar maple, yellow birch and hemlock; old beech stands often have a carpet of root-sprout saplings beneath them.
species.identify: Smooth, pale grey bark on a tall tree; long, sharp, cigar-shaped buds; oval leaves with coarse teeth and straight parallel veins, many held, bleached, through winter. The nuts are small, three-sided and come two to a soft-bristled husk that splits into four.
species.use: Gather freshly fallen husks after the first hard frosts and shell the nuts; roast them lightly before eating more than a handful, since raw beechnuts in quantity upset the stomach. Big crops come only every few years — take a modest share and leave the rest for bears, turkeys and jays.
species.lookalikes: Horse chestnut and buckeye (Aesculus) drop big glossy brown nuts with a pale eye from a smooth or spiny leathery husk, one or two to a husk, and they are poisonous. A beechnut is tiny, sharply triangular and sits in pairs inside a soft-prickled four-part husk. Chestnut burrs are far larger and viciously spiny.
species.caution: Many large beeches across the east are dying of beech bark disease and, more recently, beech leaf disease; sick trees make few nuts, and many husks are empty. Never eat a quantity raw.

species.name: Eastern white pine
species.habitat: Sandy and rocky soils, old fields, lake shores and mixed forest from the Maritimes to Minnesota; the tallest tree in most eastern woods, and a common planted tree far beyond that.
species.identify: Soft, flexible, bluish-green needles in bundles of five — the only eastern pine with five — and long, slender, curved cones with resin-tipped scales. Horizontal whorls of branches give old trees a layered look.
species.use: A small handful of chopped fresh needles steeped, not boiled, for a resinous tea; the spring pollen can be shaken into flour; the inner bark is a famine food, not a treat. Snip needles from several branches rather than stripping one.
species.lookalikes: Yew (Taxus) is the deadly one: flat, dark, single needles in two rows, a red fleshy cup around each seed instead of a cone, and every part except that red flesh can stop the heart. Pine needles are long, three-sided, and always in bundles. Norfolk Island pine and Australian pine are not pines at all — if the needles are not in bundles, do not make tea.
species.caution: Needles of ponderosa, lodgepole and some other pines cause late-term abortion in cattle; there is no good human evidence either way, so the long-standing advice is that pregnant people skip pine-needle tea. Keep to small amounts of white pine and never use yew, which can grow as a hedge beside it.

species.name: Black cherry
species.habitat: Fence lines, roadsides, old fields and the edges of hardwood forest; one of the first trees to seed into an abandoned pasture.
species.identify: A tall tree — the only cherry that grows to timber size — with young bark banded by horizontal pores and old bark broken into dark ‘burnt potato chip’ plates. Turn a leaf over: a line of rusty hairs runs along the base of the midrib. A snapped twig smells of bitter almond.
species.use: The dark, bittersweet cherries, strained for syrup, jelly, juice and wine; spit out or sieve every pit. Pick from low branches by hand and never break limbs — wilted cherry leaves kill grazing animals.
species.lookalikes: Common buckthorn is the dangerous twin: black berries clustered along the twig at the leaf joints instead of in hanging chains, a short thorn at the tip of most twigs, no almond smell, and a fruit that acts as a violent purgative. Chokecherry is a shrub or small tree with denser, more astringent clusters and is edible too; pin cherry has bright red fruit on long stalks and is also edible.
species.caution: The pits, leaves, bark and twigs contain cyanide-forming compounds, and wilted leaves are the most dangerous of all. Eat only the flesh of the ripe fruit.

species.name: Wild plums
species.habitat: Thickets on fence lines, coulees, riverbanks, pasture edges and roadsides, spreading by root suckers into dense stands; Chickasaw plum favours sandy ground in the south.
species.identify: A thorny shrub or small tree that flowers white before the leaves, with short spur branches ending in a sharp point. Fruit a true plum, 2–3 cm (1 in), red, orange or yellow with a whitish bloom and a single flattened stone.
species.use: Eat the ripe flesh fresh, or simmer and sieve for jam, fruit leather and sauce; the skins are tart and the stones are discarded. Take from a thicket, not a lone tree, and leave plenty — plum thickets feed everything from grouse to foxes.
species.lookalikes: Common buckthorn has black four-seeded berries, not a single-stoned red or yellow plum, and its berries are a harsh purgative. Hawthorn haws are edible but have several hard seeds, and hawthorn thorns are long, shiny and unbranched. Crabapples have a core of small seeds, never a stone.
species.caution: The stone and leaves contain cyanide-forming compounds; do not crack the pits for the kernels. Plums on a neighbour’s fence line belong to the neighbour.

species.name: Black locust flowers
species.habitat: Native to the Appalachians and Ozarks, now planted and run wild on roadsides, railway banks, old fields and city edges across the continent.
species.identify: Only the flowers are food: hanging 10–20 cm (4–8 in) clusters of white, sweet-scented pea flowers in late May or June on a deeply furrowed tree with feathery compound leaves and a pair of short spines at the base of each leaf.
species.use: Pull the open flowers off the stems and eat them fresh, dip whole clusters in batter for fritters, or steep them for syrup and cordial. The window is one to two weeks; pick from several trees and never strip a branch.
species.lookalikes: Wisteria hangs similar racemes, usually purple but sometimes white, from a twining vine, not a tree, and its seeds and pods are poisonous. Honey locust has branched thorns on the trunk, no showy white flowers, and long twisted pods; bristly locust is a pink-flowered shrub. Redbud has heart-shaped leaves and magenta flowers tight to the bark.
species.caution: The bark, leaves, seeds and wood of black locust are poisonous — children have been poisoned chewing the bark and horses have died of it. Eat the flowers only, and only once they are open. Invasive in parts of the Midwest and West.

set.habitat: Native to the Appalachians and Ozarks of North America; look on roadsides, railway banks, old fields and city edges.
set.caution: The bark, leaves, seeds and wood of black locust are poisonous — children have been poisoned chewing the bark and horses have died of it. Eat the flowers only, and only once they are open.

species.name: Redbud flowers
species.habitat: Woodland edges, stream banks and limestone slopes as an understory tree in the east; in Canada truly wild only on Pelee Island, but planted in gardens and streets wherever it will survive the winter.
species.identify: Small magenta-pink pea flowers growing straight out of the bare twigs, branches and even the trunk in April or May, before the heart-shaped leaves open. Flat bean-like pods follow and hang on through winter.
species.use: Buds and open flowers raw in salads, pickled like capers, or folded into pancakes; the very young, flat green pods can be cooked like snow peas. Pinch off a few clusters per branch — the flowers are the tree’s seed crop and its bees’ first meal.
species.lookalikes: Flowering crab and ornamental cherries bloom pink at the same time, but their flowers sit on stalks at the twig tips and open with or after the leaves. Nothing else here puts pea flowers directly on old bark. Judas tree (Cercis siliquastrum) is the planted European relative and is used the same way.
species.caution: Ontario’s wild redbuds are a tiny population — enjoy a planted one instead. Avoid trees in sprayed yards and parks.

species.name: Mayapple
species.habitat: Rich, moist deciduous woods, wooded slopes and riverbanks, spreading by rhizome into colonies of hundreds of umbrella leaves.
species.identify: Knee-high colonies of one or two deeply lobed umbrella leaves per stalk; the two-leaved plants hold a single nodding white flower in the fork in spring and one egg-shaped fruit in summer. Only a soft, yellow, strongly fragrant fruit that comes away in your hand is ripe.
species.use: The ripe flesh only, pressed through a sieve to remove the seeds and skin, for a lemon-and-pineapple juice, jelly or a spoonful eaten fresh. Keep to a few; even the ripe fruit disagrees with some people in quantity.
species.lookalikes: Nothing else in these woods makes an umbrella leaf — the danger is the plant itself. A green, hard fruit, the rind, the seeds, the leaves and the roots all contain podophyllotoxin and are poisonous; so is an unripe fruit a child picks because it looks like a small green apple. Fully ripe means yellow, soft, fragrant, usually fallen.
species.caution: Every part except the ripe fruit flesh is poisonous and handling the root can inflame the skin. Pick nothing green. Leave most fruit for box turtles, which spread the seed.

species.name: Spicebush
species.habitat: Damp, rich understory — stream sides, floodplain woods, ravines and the shady feet of slopes — often the commonest shrub there.
species.identify: A loose understory shrub with smooth-edged oval leaves and fine white dots on the twigs; scratch a twig and it smells sharply of lemon and allspice. Tiny yellow flowers hug the bare twigs in early spring, and female shrubs carry glossy red oval berries in September.
species.use: Twigs and leaves steeped for tea in any month; the red berries picked in September, dried whole and ground as a hot, allspice-like seasoning. Snip twig tips from several bushes; only female plants fruit, so leave some berries to grow new ones.
species.lookalikes: Bush honeysuckle (Lonicera) hangs red berries in pairs at the leaf joints on hollow twigs with no smell, and the berries are mildly poisonous. Winterberry holly holds red berries tight to the twig into winter and is poisonous, with toothed leaves and no scent. The spicebush smell rules both out: no spice, no spicebush.
species.caution: Spicebush swallowtail caterpillars live in the folded leaves — leave them. Harvesting is prohibited in most parks.

species.name: Sassafras
species.habitat: Old fields, fencerows, sandy woods and roadsides, suckering into thickets; a small tree in the north and a real tree in the south.
species.identify: Three leaf shapes on one tree — plain oval, three-lobed, and a one-thumbed ‘mitten’ — on green twigs that smell of root beer when scratched. Female trees carry dark blue berries in red cups in autumn.
species.use: Young leaves dried and ground are filé, the Choctaw thickener for gumbo, and are the part to favour. Root-bark tea is the famous use, but the root contains safrole and is restricted as food in the US; if you make it at all, make it rarely and weak.
species.lookalikes: Red mulberry can show mitten leaves too, but its leaves are toothed and its twigs bleed milky sap when broken, with no root-beer smell. Young tulip trees have four-pointed, squared-off leaves. Spicebush shares the spicy smell but has unlobed leaves and red berries.
species.caution: Safrole, concentrated in the root bark, caused liver cancer in laboratory animals and the US FDA bans it and sassafras bark as a food ingredient; the leaves contain little or none. Do not give root tea to children or drink it in pregnancy.

species.name: Autumn olive
species.habitat: Old fields, roadsides, highway banks, reclaimed mines and pasture edges — anywhere it was planted for ‘wildlife’ in the last century and everywhere birds have carried it since.
species.identify: A sprawling thorny shrub whose leaves flash silver underneath; in autumn it is weighed down with small red berries finely speckled with silver and brown scales, each with one soft seed.
species.use: Eat the berries once they are fully red and soft after a frost — before that they pucker the mouth; run them through a food mill for juice, fruit leather, sauce and jam. Pick as many as you like: it is invasive wherever it grows, and every berry you take is one a bird does not plant.
species.lookalikes: Bush honeysuckle berries are red but glossy and unspeckled, hang in pairs, and are mildly poisonous; its leaves are green beneath, not silver. Common buckthorn has black berries and no silver. Russian olive, its western cousin, has narrower willow-like leaves and mealy silver-yellow fruit, and is also edible.
species.caution: Berries from roadsides and old mine sites can carry road salt and metals the shrub pulls from the soil; pick away from traffic. Do not plant it or move the seed — it is a restricted invasive in several states and spreading in Ontario and the Maritimes.

species.name: Fireweed
species.habitat: Burns, clear-cuts, roadsides, avalanche tracks and river gravels — any open, disturbed ground in the north and the mountains, often in sheets that turn a hillside magenta.
species.identify: A tall unbranched spire, 1–2 m (3–6 ft), of four-petalled magenta flowers opening from the bottom up; narrow alternate leaves on a round, often reddish stem. Hold a leaf to the light: the side veins curve and join into a line running just inside the edge, which no look-alike shares.
species.use: Young shoots in spring, snapped where they break cleanly and steamed like asparagus; flowers and buds in July–August for jelly, syrup and a floral honey. Take shoots from a big patch and leave most standing — the plant feeds the whole clearing.
species.lookalikes: Purple loosestrife is the summer double: an invasive wetland plant with a square stem, opposite leaves and five- to seven-petalled flowers packed in a tighter, darker spike. It is not poisonous but it is not food. In spring the shoots can be confused with dogbane and milkweed shoots, which bleed milky sap when snapped — fireweed’s sap is clear.
species.caution: Mature leaves and strong tea can be mildly laxative; start with a little. Fireweed is the floral emblem of Yukon and is protected in parks like everything else, but it is abundant and picking a few shoots on a roadside harms nothing.

species.name: Lingonberry (partridgeberry)
species.habitat: Acidic, well-drained ground: open spruce and pine woods, rock outcrops, bog hummocks and tundra, usually in a dense ankle-high mat.
species.identify: A creeping evergreen 5–20 cm (2–8 in) tall with small, thick, glossy oval leaves whose edges roll under; turn a leaf over and look for scattered dark bristly dots on the pale underside. Firm red berries hang in small clusters at the branch tips, and the tiny bell flowers that preceded them had four fused petals.
species.use: Tart and firm — sauce, jam, juice and the Newfoundland partridgeberry pie; they keep for months cold. Pick after the first frost, when they sweeten and loosen, and rake with your fingers rather than tearing the mat.
species.lookalikes: Bearberry (kinnikinnick) is the common double: red berries on a trailing evergreen of sandy, rocky ground, with no dots under the leaf and urn-shaped five-petalled flowers; its berries are edible but dry and mealy. Red baneberry is the toxic red berry of the same woods — but it is a soft leafy herb with compound leaves and berries in a stalked cluster, never an evergreen mat.
species.caution: Check the whole plant, not just the berry: a low evergreen mat with dotted leaves, never a leafy herb. Picking is prohibited in most parks and reserves.

set.habitat: Acidic, well-drained ground: coastal barrens and headlands in Newfoundland, open spruce and pine woods, rock outcrops, bog hummocks and tundra, usually in a dense ankle-high mat.

set.name: Lingonberry
set.use: Tart and firm — sauce, jam and juice; they keep for months cold. Pick after the first frost, when they sweeten and loosen, and rake with your fingers rather than tearing the mat.

set.name: Lingonberry
set.habitat: Acidic, well-drained ground: open spruce and pine woods, rock outcrops, bog hummocks and tundra, usually in a dense ankle-high mat.
set.use: Tart and firm — sauce, jam and juice; they keep for months cold. Pick after the first frost, when they sweeten and loosen, and rake with your fingers rather than tearing the mat.

species.name: Cloudberry (bakeapple)
species.habitat: Open sphagnum bogs, muskeg and wet tundra, where the plants carpet the moss between stunted black spruce and tamarack.
species.identify: A single stalk 10–25 cm (4–10 in) tall with two or three rounded leaves of five to seven shallow lobes, one white five-petalled flower, and one berry — no thorns, no canes. The berry starts hard and red and ripens to soft, translucent amber, which is the only stage to pick.
species.use: Eaten fresh, or as the bakeapple jam, sauce and cheesecake topping of Newfoundland and Labrador; a few hours of picking fills a small bucket. Take only soft amber berries, step on the moss lightly, and leave the green and red ones for the next picker and the birds.
species.lookalikes: Nagoonberry (arctic dwarf raspberry, Rubus arcticus) grows in the same bogs with a pink flower and a red berry; it is edible and better-tasting, so the mix-up costs nothing. A red cloudberry is simply unripe. In western Alaska this plant is called salmonberry, a name that elsewhere belongs to a tall thorny shrub (R. spectabilis) — ask which one is meant.
species.caution: Cloudberry patches are family picking grounds in Newfoundland and Labrador, Nunavik and Nunatsiavut; do not strip a bog near a community. Listed as threatened at the southern edge of its range (Minnesota), where it should be left alone.

set.name: Cloudberry
set.use: Eaten fresh, or as jam and sauce; a few hours of picking fills a small bucket. Take only soft amber berries, step on the moss lightly, and leave the green and red ones for the next picker and the birds.

set.name: Cloudberry
set.use: Eaten fresh, or as jam and sauce; a few hours of picking fills a small bucket. Take only soft amber berries, step on the moss lightly, and leave the green and red ones for the next picker and the birds.
set.lookalikes: Arctic dwarf raspberry (Rubus arcticus) grows in the same bogs with a pink flower and a red berry; it is edible and better-tasting, so the mix-up costs nothing. A red cloudberry is simply unripe.

species.name: Labrador tea
species.habitat: Sphagnum bogs, muskeg, wet black-spruce woods and acid lakeshores, often shoulder to shoulder with the poisonous bog laurel it is mistaken for.
species.identify: A knee-high evergreen shrub whose leathery, alternate leaves have edges rolled under and a thick rusty-orange wool on the underside — dense, felted and unmistakable on mature leaves. White flowers in rounded clusters in June. No rusty wool, no Labrador tea.
species.use: Only the leaves, and only as a weak tea in moderation: a few leaves per cup, boiling water poured over and steeped 5–10 minutes, never boiled or stewed. A traditional beverage of Cree, Innu and Inuit households across the north. Pick a few leaves from each plant.
species.lookalikes: Bog laurel (Kalmia polifolia) and sheep laurel (K. angustifolia) are poisonous and share the bog: opposite or whorled leaves that are smooth, pale or whitish beneath — never rusty-woolly — and pink saucer-shaped flowers. Bog rosemary (Andromeda polifolia) is also toxic: narrow blue-green leaves with a powdery white underside and pink urn-shaped flowers. White flowers and orange wool, or leave it.
species.caution: Labrador tea contains ledol and grayanotoxins; strong or boiled tea, or many cups, can cause vomiting, dizziness, slowed pulse and worse. Avoid in pregnancy and for young children. Check every leaf you pick, not just the first plant.

species.name: Bunchberry
species.habitat: Cool, acidic conifer and mixed woods, mossy logs, bog edges and subalpine slopes, in carpets across the forest floor.
species.identify: A 10–20 cm (4–8 in) plant with a single whorl of four to six oval leaves whose veins arch toward the tip like a dogwood’s; in June the four white ‘petals’ are bracts around a knot of tiny flowers, and by August a tight bunch of bright red berries sits in the middle of the whorl.
species.use: Edible once identified, but bland and mealy with a hard seed — a trail nibble and a safe first berry for children to learn on, better in a mixed jam than alone. Take a few berries from a carpet; the plant spreads by rhizome and is in no danger.
species.lookalikes: Red baneberry (Actaea rubra) is the poisonous red berry of the same woods: a bushy herb to 60 cm (2 ft) with large compound, toothed leaves and glossy berries, each with a black dot, in a cluster held on a stalk above the leaves. Bunchberry’s berries sit directly in a whorl of simple leaves on an ankle-high plant; the whole shape rules baneberry out.
species.caution: Teach children the whorl-of-leaves rule before the berry rule. Baneberry’s berries can slow the heart; a few are enough to send a child to hospital.

species.name: Wild currants and gooseberries
species.habitat: Moist woods, streambanks, swamp edges, coulees and fence lines in the east; canyons, river bottoms and mountain slopes in the west.
species.identify: A shrub 1–2 m (3–6 ft) tall with maple-like lobed leaves, and berries that each keep a dried flower ‘tail’ at the tip. Currants are thornless with six or more berries in a dangling chain; gooseberries carry spines at the leaf nodes and hold one to four berries, often bristly.
species.use: Black currants for jam and cordial, red and golden currants for jelly, gooseberries stewed or in pie. Pick ripe berries in July–August — soft, fully coloured and coming away easily — and leave the bush standing.
species.lookalikes: The confusables are red berries without the tail: red baneberry (poisonous), a soft-stemmed herb with compound leaves and a stalked cluster of glossy berries, each with a black dot; and bush honeysuckle (Lonicera), with untoothed opposite leaves and berries in pairs that cause vomiting. A lobed leaf and a tailed berry on a woody stem is a Ribes.
species.caution: Skunk currant (R. glandulosum) is edible but smells of skunk when handled. Ribes hosts white pine blister rust; Maine, New Hampshire, Massachusetts and Rhode Island still restrict planting them, which does not stop you picking wild ones. Expect bristly fruit on prickly gooseberry.
