species.name: Nodding onion
species.habitat: Dry open woods, rocky bluffs, prairie remnants, mountain meadows and Garry oak slopes — sunny, well-drained ground.
species.identify: A clump of flat, grass-like leaves from a slender bulb, and in July–August a stem that bends sharply at the top so the pink umbel of bell flowers hangs downward. Crush a leaf: the whole plant smells strongly of onion. No onion smell means it is not an onion, whatever else it looks like.
species.use: Leaves and flowers raw or cooked wherever chives go; the small bulbs are strong and sweet when cooked. Snip a few leaves from each clump and leave the bulbs — a dug bulb is a dead plant, and the patches are slow to spread.
species.lookalikes: Death camas (Toxicoscordion venenosum and relatives) grows in the same meadows with the same grass-like leaves and a similar bulb, and it kills. Its flowers are cream-white in an upright spike, not pink and nodding, and no part of it smells of onion. Smell every plant you cut.
species.caution: Listed as special concern in Minnesota and uncommon across much of the east; take leaves, not plants. Dogs and cats should not be fed any Allium.

species.name: Camas
species.habitat: Meadows and prairies that are wet in spring and dry by midsummer: Garry oak savannah, vernal swales, Palouse grassland and mountain meadows, in sheets that look like standing water when in bloom.
species.identify: Grass-like basal leaves and an upright spike of starry six-petalled blue to violet flowers in April–June; the bulb below is a plain white onion-shape with no smell. Mark plants while they are in flower and dig only those — the bulb alone cannot be told from death camas.
species.use: The bulb, dug after the flowers fade in June–July and traditionally pit-roasted for 24–48 hours until dark and sweet; raw or briefly cooked it is starchy and gassy because its inulin has not broken down. This is a keystone food of Coast Salish, Nez Perce, Kalapuya and other Plateau and Northwest peoples, who tended camas prairies for millennia. Harvest only on private land with an invitation, and leave wild meadows to those with rights and knowledge.
species.lookalikes: Death camas (Toxicoscordion venenosum) grows bulb to bulb with camas and has killed people who dug by the bulb. Its flowers are cream-white in a denser spike; camas flowers are blue. Identify and flag every plant in bloom, dig nothing you did not flag, and discard any bulb you are unsure of.
species.caution: Camas prairies are rare and culturally significant; most are protected, and digging in parks and reserves is illegal. Many documented poisonings come from this one confusion. Not a plant for a first-time forager.

species.name: Oregon grape
species.habitat: Douglas-fir and pine understory, rocky slopes, road cuts and city plantings from sea level into the mountains; the creeping species carpet dry open forest in the Rockies.
species.identify: An evergreen shrub with holly-like pinnate leaves of five to nine spiny-edged leaflets, upright clusters of yellow flowers in spring, and powdery blue-black berries in grape-like bunches by late summer. Scrape a stem: the inner bark and wood are bright yellow.
species.use: Very tart — jelly, juice and syrup, usually sweetened or blended with salal or other berries; a traditional mixer for Coast and Plateau peoples. Pick the whole cluster when the berries are dusty blue and soft, and leave plenty for the birds.
species.lookalikes: True hollies (Ilex) have the same spiny leaves but each leaf is single, not a row of leaflets, and the berries are red and in the leaf axils; holly berries cause vomiting. Nothing with blue berries in grape-like clusters on a yellow-wooded, pinnate-leaved shrub is anything but a Berberis.
species.caution: Oregon grape contains berberine, bitter and in quantity upsetting to the stomach, especially for children; tradition and herbal references both avoid it in pregnancy. Eat the berries in sauce and jelly rather than by the handful. Oregon’s state flower and protected in parks.

species.name: Pinyon pine nuts (piñon)
species.habitat: Dry rocky foothills and mesas at 1,400–2,300 m (4,500–7,500 ft), in open pinyon–juniper woodland between the sagebrush and the ponderosa belt.
species.identify: A short, rounded, often multi-trunked pine 3–9 m (10–30 ft) tall with stiff needles in twos (single-leaf pinyon has them singly); small round cones 4–5 cm (1½–2 in) with thick scales that open in September–October to drop large, thin-shelled brown seeds.
species.use: The seeds, gathered from opened cones or from a tarp spread under a shaken tree, then dried, roasted in the shell and cracked. Mast years come every three to seven years; a good crop is announced locally. Never cut limbs or knock green cones.
species.lookalikes: Every other pine has edible seeds, so the confusion is harmless, but most are too small to bother with. The one evergreen to know is yew — flat needles in two rows, red fleshy cups instead of cones, every part but the red flesh deadly — though it does not grow in pinyon country. ‘Pine mouth’, a bitter metallic taste lasting days, comes from certain imported Asian pine nuts (Pinus armandii), not from pinyon.
species.caution: Personal-use limits apply on National Forest and BLM land (commonly 25 lb per household per season free, more only by permit) and Tribal lands are closed to outsiders; piñon picking is a family tradition for Diné (Navajo), Shoshone and Paiute communities whose harvest areas should be respected. Tree nut allergy applies.

species.name: Wild garlic (ramsons)
species.habitat: Damp, shady deciduous woods, stream banks and old hedgerows, often carpeting the ground in spring — an ancient-woodland plant.
species.identify: Broad, bright green, smooth-edged leaves up to 25 cm (10 in) long, each on its own slender stalk straight from the ground, and a strong garlic smell from every crushed leaf. From April, round heads of white star-shaped flowers on a leafless stalk.
species.use: Leaves raw or wilted — pesto, soup, butter, cheese — best before the flowers open; the flowers and green seed heads are good too. Cut leaves and leave the bulbs in the ground.
species.lookalikes: Lily of the valley, autumn crocus (meadow saffron) and lords-and-ladies come up in the same places, and every spring people in Europe are poisoned after picking them as wild garlic; autumn crocus has killed. Lily of the valley has two or three duller leaves wrapped round one stem; autumn crocus makes a stalkless tuft; arum leaves are arrow-shaped and net-veined. None of them smells of garlic.
species.caution: Crush and smell every leaf, not just the first — once your fingers smell of garlic, everything will. Never grab handfuls from a mixed patch.

species.name: Mediterranean wild asparagus
species.habitat: Dry, sunny scrub, olive groves, woodland edges and old walls, mainly on limestone, from the coast up to about 1,300 m (4,300 ft).
species.identify: An evergreen, scrambling clump of stiff, sharply pointed, needle-like ‘leaves’. After the winter rains, thin dark green to purplish spears — pencil-thin or thinner — push up through last year’s prickly tangle.
species.use: Snap each spear where it breaks cleanly. Strong and slightly bitter: scrambled with eggs, the classic way in Spain, Italy and Croatia, or in risotto. Leave some spears on every plant.
species.lookalikes: Black bryony sends up thin shoots in the same scrub; it is a twining vine with glossy heart-shaped leaves, and its berries and roots are poisonous — leave any shoot that twines. Other wild asparagus species and butcher’s broom also grow there; pick only where you can see the old asparagus needles.
species.caution: The needles are sharp: gloves and long sleeves.

species.name: Common sorrel
species.habitat: Meadows, pastures, road verges, woodland edges and upland grassland — common almost everywhere in Europe.
species.identify: Arrow-shaped leaves whose two base lobes point straight back, a thin papery sheath where each leaf meets the stem, and a sharp lemon-sour taste. In early summer, slender spikes of tiny reddish flowers up to 60 cm (2 ft) tall.
species.use: Young leaves in salad, sorrel soup, and the classic sharp sauce for salmon and other fish. Cook only briefly — it turns khaki and melts.
species.lookalikes: Young lords-and-ladies leaves are arrow-shaped too and come up in the same hedge banks. They are glossier, with wavy edges, a net of veins and often dark spots, and they burn the mouth at once. Sheep sorrel is a smaller, edible cousin.
species.caution: High in oxalic acid: a herb and a sauce, not a daily salad bowl, and best avoided by anyone prone to kidney stones.

species.name: St George’s mushroom
species.habitat: Grassland — chalk and limestone downs, pastures, mown verges and woodland edges — often in rings or arcs that return to the same spot for decades.
species.identify: A stocky, white to cream mushroom with a thick, smooth cap 5–15 cm (2–6 in) across, crowded narrow white gills, a fat stem with no ring, a white spore print, and a strong smell of wet flour or cucumber. It is up in spring, when few large pale mushrooms are.
species.use: Firm and mealy raw; cooking turns the floury smell into a rich flavour. Fried in butter, or in an omelette as in Bilbao.
species.lookalikes: The deadly fibrecap fruits in late spring and summer in the same places: its cap is conical and silky-streaked, bruises and ages brick-red, and it drops a brown spore print. It has killed. Livid entoloma (later in the year, with pinkish gills and a pink print) and the small white lawn funnels (summer and autumn, gills running down the stem) are poisonous too.
species.caution: Take a spore print of your first finds and of any that stain red. White print, mealy smell, no reddening — and still check every one.

species.name: Yellow morel
species.habitat: Old orchards, river woods under ash and elm, hedgerows, copses, parks and disturbed ground, often on chalky soil.
species.identify: A pale cream to yellow-brown, sponge-like cap of irregular pits with paler ridges, joined to the stem at its lower edge. Slice it top to bottom: one continuous hollow from cap tip to stem base.
species.use: Always cooked through. Halve, rinse out the grit and insects, then sauté in butter; dried morels make the classic cream sauce.
species.lookalikes: False morel has a lobed, brain-like cap, is chambered or cottony inside, grows on sandy soil under pine, and can kill. Thimble morel’s cap hangs free like a skirt. Stinkhorn eggs and stinkhorns smell foul and sit in a cup at the base.
species.caution: Raw morels are poisonous. Slice every one lengthwise before it goes in the basket.

species.name: Birch sap
species.habitat: Birch woods, heaths and parks — silver and downy birch, on any big, healthy tree.
species.identify: Silver birch has white, papery bark that cracks into black diamonds at the base and drooping twig tips; downy birch has duller bark and upright, downy twigs. Both are tapped. The sap runs for a few weeks in early spring, before the leaves open.
species.use: Drunk fresh — clear, faintly sweet and silky. It sours within two or three days, so drink it, freeze it, or let it ferment.
species.lookalikes: Tap only trees you can name by their bark in bare-branched spring. Birch sap is the drink; most other trees’ sap is not.
species.caution: Tapping wounds the tree and lets in decay. One small hole in a big, healthy birch, plugged afterwards — and only with the landowner’s permission: everyman’s right covers berries and mushrooms, not tapping trees.

species.name: Elderflower (European elder)
species.habitat: Hedgerows, woodland edges, scrub, riverbanks, railway banks and waste ground — anywhere rich and disturbed.
species.identify: A woody shrub or small tree with corky, furrowed grey-brown bark and opposite leaves of five to seven toothed leaflets; flat, creamy-white heads of tiny five-petalled flowers up to 24 cm (9 in) across, with a heavy sweet scent.
species.use: Cordial, sparkling elderflower, fritters and syrup. Pick fresh, fully open heads on a dry morning, shake out the insects, and don’t wash away the pollen.
species.lookalikes: Hemlock, hemlock water-dropwort and cow parsley also carry white umbrella-shaped heads, but they are soft green herbs with no bark — elder is a woody shrub. Dwarf elder is a poisonous elder that dies back to the ground every winter, grows in leafy patches and smells foul when its leaves are crushed.
species.caution: Only the flowers: leaves, stems and bark are poisonous. Snip the flowers off the thick stalks before steeping.

species.name: Sweet cicely
species.habitat: Mountain meadows and woodland margins in the Alps and other southern ranges; in Britain, verges, stream banks and woodland edges, most often in northern England and Scotland.
species.identify: A soft, downy, fern-like plant to 1–2 m (3–6 ft) with finely divided pale green leaves, often flecked white, and a strong sweet smell of aniseed when crushed. White flower heads in April–June, then long, slender, ridged seeds 15–25 mm (⅝–1 in), green at first and glossy dark brown when ripe.
species.use: Leaves chopped into salads or cooked with sour fruit such as rhubarb to soften it; the green seeds chewed as an aniseed sweet; the root cooked like parsnip.
species.lookalikes: It belongs to the carrot family, which holds Europe’s deadliest plants. Hemlock (hairless, purple-blotched stem, mousy smell) and hemlock water-dropwort (hairless, in wet ground, smelling deceptively of parsley or celery) grow near it, and cow parsley and fool’s parsley are close in leaf. Only the full set — downy leaves, a strong aniseed smell and those long seeds — says sweet cicely.
species.caution: Not a beginner’s plant. Learn it in seed, with someone who knows it, before you eat a leaf — and don’t trust your nose after handling it, because the aniseed stays on your fingers.

species.name: Marsh samphire
species.habitat: Open mud and sand of salt marshes and estuaries, washed by the tide, often in wide green swards on the lower marsh.
species.identify: A low, leafless, jointed succulent 10–30 cm (4–12 in) tall, like a tiny branching cactus: bright glassy green, very salty, and it snaps cleanly. It turns red or purple in autumn.
species.use: Snip the tender green tips, rinse out the mud, then boil or steam a few minutes in unsalted water and toss in butter. Good raw or pickled too.
species.lookalikes: Annual sea-blite grows in the same mud and is eaten too, but it has small, fleshy, pointed leaves where samphire has smooth, leafless, snap-apart joints. Whatever you pick, the real risk is the water it grew in — stay away from outfalls.
species.caution: Cut, don’t pull: in Britain it is an offence to uproot any wild plant without the landowner’s permission, and many salt marshes are protected. Pick away from outfalls and harbours, and watch the tide.

species.name: Sea beet (wild spinach)
species.habitat: The top of sand and shingle beaches, sea walls, cliffs, salt-marsh drift lines and waste ground near the sea.
species.identify: A sprawling, leafy perennial with dark green, glossy, leathery leaves — the lower ones wavy-edged and roughly triangular — often on reddish stems, and in summer thick, grooved spikes of tiny green flowers. It looks and tastes like a wild chard.
species.use: Young leaves raw; bigger ones stripped of their stems and wilted like spinach. Take a few leaves from each plant and it keeps producing.
species.lookalikes: Oraches and sea purslane share the strandline and are eaten too, but their leaves are mealy or silvery-grey, where sea beet’s are dark, glossy and leathery. Away from the shore, learn it in flower first — the thick spikes of tiny green flowers settle it.
species.caution: Like spinach and chard it holds oxalate — a vegetable, not a daily bucketful. Pick away from outfalls and dog-walking paths.

species.name: Woodland strawberry
species.habitat: Woodland edges and clearings, banks, hedge bottoms, trail sides and limestone grassland — often in dappled light.
species.identify: Three shiny, toothed leaflets on hairy stalks; white five-petalled flowers whose rounded petals touch; and small red berries about 1 cm (⅜ in) long with the seeds on the surface. On the end leaflet, the tip tooth is as long as or longer than the teeth beside it.
species.use: Eat them where they grow — they bruise in minutes. A handful scents a whole bowl of cream.
species.lookalikes: Barren strawberry flowers in early spring with gappy, notch-tipped petals, has duller leaves whose end tooth is shorter than its neighbours, and never makes a red berry. Yellow-flowered mock strawberry makes a bland one. Neither is harmful.

species.name: Chanterelle (girolle)
species.habitat: Mossy birch, oak, beech and conifer woods on acid soil, often beside paths, coming back to the same spots for years.
species.identify: Egg-yolk yellow, firm and solid, with a wavy cap and blunt, forking ridges — not true gills — running down the stem like melted wax. Pale flesh inside, a fruity apricot smell, and it grows from the soil, never from wood.
species.use: Brush clean; dry-fry to drive off the water, then butter, garlic and parsley. Freeze them cooked — oven-drying makes them bitter.
species.lookalikes: False chanterelle is more orange and softer, with thin, true gills that fork. The Mediterranean jack-o’-lantern grows in clusters on stumps and olive roots, with sharp true gills and orange flesh right through. Worst are the deadly webcaps — rusty-brown, with true gills and a rusty spore print — which have been picked as chanterelles in Scotland and Austria and destroyed people’s kidneys.
species.caution: Check every mushroom, not just the first: ridges not gills, solid pale flesh, apricot smell, growing from the ground.

species.name: Bilberry
species.habitat: Acid soil under pine, spruce, birch and oak, and on heath and moorland, often carpeting the forest floor from the lowlands to the treeline.
species.identify: A knee-high shrub with bright green, angled stems and small, finely toothed oval leaves. Blue-black berries with a dusty bloom hang one per stalk, each with a little crown at the tip — and the flesh is purple-red right through, staining fingers and tongue.
species.use: By the handful, or in pies, tarts, jam, soup and juice. Spread them on a tray to freeze the day you pick.
species.lookalikes: Deadly nightshade has shiny black berries of a similar size, but singly on a branching herb up to 1.5 m (5 ft) tall, each sitting in a green five-pointed star. Bog bilberry (edible) has blue-green untoothed leaves and pale flesh; herb Paris holds a single poisonous blue-black berry above a ring of four leaves. Pick only from the low, green-stemmed shrub.

species.name: Rowan berries
species.habitat: Upland woods, moorland edges, rocky ground and city streets; up to the treeline in the Alps and far north in Norway.
species.identify: A slim tree with smooth silvery-grey bark and feathery leaves of many toothed leaflets in pairs; big flat clusters of scarlet-orange berries, each about 1 cm (⅜ in) across with a tiny black five-pointed star at the tip.
species.use: Cooked, never raw by the handful: tart jelly (the classic with game and lamb), jam, syrup and chutney. Freezing, cooking or drying breaks down the bitterness.
species.lookalikes: Ash and elder also have feathery compound leaves, but neither carries big flat heads of orange berries — ash has winged seeds, and elder’s leaves are opposite with fewer leaflets. Cotoneaster, guelder rose and yew carry red fruit on simple leaves.
species.caution: Raw berries contain parasorbic acid, which irritates the stomach and acts as a laxative — always cook them.

species.name: Sea buckthorn
species.habitat: Coastal dunes and cliffs of the North Sea and Baltic, river gravels in the Alps, and dry slopes in the Carpathians, often in dense thickets.
species.identify: A thorny shrub with narrow, silvery-grey, willow-like leaves and branches packed with bright orange berries 6–8 mm (¼ in) across, from late summer into winter. Only female bushes fruit.
species.use: Fiercely sour and rich in vitamin C: juice, jelly and syrup, or mixed with sweeter fruit. The berries burst when pulled, so many pickers snip a few laden twigs, freeze them, and knock the frozen berries off.
species.lookalikes: Few shrubs carry orange berries packed along thorny, silver-leaved twigs. Firethorn, a garden shrub, has orange-red berries in clusters among glossy green leaves and is not one to pick for food.
species.caution: Thick gloves — the thorns are long and sharp. Snip twigs sparingly.

species.name: Elderberries (European elder)
species.habitat: The same hedges, scrub and waste ground where the shrubs flowered in June.
species.identify: Drooping, flat-topped clusters of glossy purple-black berries 6–8 mm (¼ in) across on purple-red stalks, on a woody shrub with corky bark and opposite compound leaves.
species.use: Always cooked: syrup, jelly, chutney, wine, Germany’s elderberry soup, and with apples or blackberries in pies. Strip the berries with a fork and pick out every green stalk and unripe berry.
species.lookalikes: Dwarf elder looks like a short elder with its berry heads held upright on soft green stems that die back every winter; it is poisonous. Dogwood and privet carry black berries on shrubs with simple leaves, and deadly nightshade bears single shiny berries in a green star — none of them in a drooping, flat elder head.
species.caution: Raw berries, seeds, leaves and stems contain cyanogenic compounds that cause nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Cook them through.

species.name: Cornelian cherry
species.habitat: Woodland edges, scrub and rocky slopes, especially on limestone, in central and south-eastern Europe; planted in parks and old gardens.
species.identify: A shrub or small tree that covers itself in clusters of tiny yellow flowers in February and March, long before the leaves. Leaves opposite, oval and smooth-edged; in late summer, glossy, oblong red fruits about 2 cm (¾ in) long, each with one stone.
species.use: Wait until they are dark ruby-red, soft and dropping — before that they are astringent. Jam, syrup and sour sauces, and fruit brandies such as Romania’s cornată.
species.lookalikes: Yew also has red fruit, but it is an open-ended cup showing a deadly seed, on a conifer with needles. Honeysuckle berries come in pairs and are not food. A cornelian cherry is a solid, olive-shaped fruit on a broadleaf shrub with opposite leaves.
species.caution: Spit out the stone.

species.name: Saffron milk cap
species.habitat: Under pines on acid or sandy soil, often in big groups; the great hunting grounds are the pinewoods of Spain, Portugal, southern France, Italy and Cyprus.
species.identify: A carrot-orange cap with darker concentric rings, inrolled at first and later funnel-shaped, on a short, often hollow stem. Break it and it bleeds carrot-orange milk; bruised and handled parts slowly turn green.
species.use: Fried cap-down in olive oil with garlic and parsley, as in Spain; grilled; or salted and pickled, as in Russia and Poland. Firm and nutty, sometimes a little bitter.
species.lookalikes: Woolly milkcap, under birch, is pinker, with a shaggy, woolly rim and white, peppery milk, and it causes stomach upsets. False saffron milk cap, under spruce, has orange milk that turns wine-red within half an hour and is edible. White milk means leave it.
species.caution: A big meal can turn your urine orange-red. It is harmless — but alarming if nobody warned you.

species.name: Parasol mushroom
species.habitat: Pastures, road verges, grassy woodland clearings, dunes and seaside cliffs, alone or in rings.
species.identify: Big and tall: a cap 10–25 cm (4–10 in) across, pale with coarse brown scales and a dark central bump; a slender stem up to 40 cm (16 in) with brown snakeskin banding; a thick double-edged ring that slides up and down; free white gills and a white spore print.
species.use: Caps only — the stems are woody. Egg-and-breadcrumb and fry like a schnitzel, as in central Europe, or stuff and bake the young drumstick caps.
species.lookalikes: Small parasols (Lepiota), some deadly, look like miniature versions: never take one with a cap under 10 cm (4 in) or without the snakeskin stem. Shaggy parasols have no snakeskin and upset many people. Panther caps and other Amanitas have pale warts on a darker cap and a cup or rimmed bulb at the base, and young buttons of all of them look alike — pick only open caps.
species.caution: No single feature is enough. The whole set every time: snakeskin stem, sliding double ring, free white gills, white print, cap over 10 cm.

species.name: Black trumpet (horn of plenty)
species.habitat: Beech and oak woods on heavy, chalky or clay soil, in moss and leaf litter in damp hollows, usually in troops.
species.identify: A thin, hollow, sooty grey-black trumpet up to 10 cm (4 in) tall, cap and stem all one piece; the outer surface is paler ash-grey and smooth or faintly wrinkled, with no gills.
species.use: Split and clean out the trumpets; sauté in butter, or dry them — dried, they taste of black truffle and crumble into sauces.
species.lookalikes: The rare ashen chanterelle is the closest double — also grey, but with shallow, gill-like ridges underneath, where the black trumpet’s outer surface is smooth or just wrinkled; it is edible. Check each one is a thin, hollow funnel with no gills.

species.name: Hedgehog mushroom
species.habitat: Broadleaf and conifer woods, singly, in groups or in rings, in moss and leaf litter.
species.identify: A buff, apricot or pale orange cap, often lumpy and irregular, with soft, crowded, pale spines hanging underneath instead of gills, and firm white flesh that bruises orange.
species.use: Brush the spines clean as you pick; sauté, simmer in stock or cream, or pickle. Nutty and crunchy. Boil older, bitter ones first.
species.lookalikes: From above it can pass for a chanterelle or any pale cap, so turn every one over: soft spines underneath, never gills or ridges. The smaller, deeper-orange terracotta hedgehog has the same spines and is eaten the same way.
species.caution: Listed as vulnerable in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany — pick lightly there, if at all.

species.name: Yellowfoot (winter chanterelle)
species.habitat: Damp, mossy conifer forest on acid soil, especially spruce, often among rotting wood, in troops of hundreds or thousands.
species.identify: A small brown funnel-shaped cap 1–4 cm (½–1½ in) across, often with a hole down the middle, on a hollow, yellow to orange stem; underneath, pale greyish-yellow forked ridges, not gills, running down the stem.
species.use: Fried, in soups and sauces, or dried. A late-autumn basket-filler.
species.lookalikes: Deadly webcap grows in the same mossy conifer woods, and people in Sweden who picked it for yellowfoot lost their kidneys. A webcap has true, rusty-brown gills, a solid stem and a rusty spore print. Check that every stem is hollow and every underside ridged, not gilled.
species.caution: Never scoop them up by the handful. Pick one at a time and look underneath each.

species.name: Sloes (blackthorn)
species.habitat: Hedgerows, scrub, woodland edges and field margins, in dense thickets that spread by suckers.
species.identify: A dense, very thorny shrub with dark bark and white blossom on bare black twigs in early spring, before the leaves. In autumn, round blue-black fruits about 1 cm (⅜ in) across with a waxy blue bloom, each holding one stone.
species.use: Sloe gin, and patxaran in Navarre and the Basque Country; also jelly, chutney and wine. Far too astringent to eat raw until frost — or a night in the freezer — softens them.
species.lookalikes: Cherry plum fruits a month or two earlier, with bigger yellow or red plums, and is edible. Buckthorn has black berries with several seeds, not one stone, and is a purgative. Deadly nightshade’s black berries grow on a soft herb, not a thorny shrub.
species.caution: Like all Prunus stones, sloe stones contain cyanide-releasing compounds: strain them out and never crush them.

species.name: Sweet chestnut
species.habitat: Coppice and old woods on acid, well-drained soil, chestnut groves on the hills of southern Europe, and parkland trees.
species.identify: A big tree with long, glossy leaves edged with sharp, regular teeth, and bark that twists in spiralling ridges on old trunks. The nuts come in twos and threes inside a husk covered in dense, needle-sharp spines; each is glossy brown, flat on one side, with a pointed tuft at the tip.
species.use: Slit the shell and roast, boil, or dry and mill into flour. Choose plump, heavy nuts and leave the flat, empty ones.
species.lookalikes: Horse chestnut is the one to know: its husk has a few short, stubby spikes, it usually holds one big round conker with a pale scar and no pointed tip, and its leaves are big hands of five to seven leaflets. Conkers are poisonous.
species.caution: Learn the conker before your first harvest — horse chestnuts stand in the same parks and avenues.

species.name: Strawberry tree (arbutus)
species.habitat: Evergreen scrub, woodland and rocky hillsides around the Mediterranean and up the Atlantic coast, often on limestone or sandstone — and around Killarney in south-west Ireland.
species.identify: An evergreen shrub or small tree with glossy, toothed leaves and red-brown, peeling bark. Round, warty red fruits 1.5–2 cm (⅝–¾ in) across ripen in autumn at the same time as the next year’s clusters of creamy, bell-shaped flowers.
species.use: Eat only fully ripe — deep red and soft. Sweet, mild and gritty; best in jam, jelly, liqueur and Portugal’s medronho brandy.
species.lookalikes: The warty skin, and white bell-flowers on the same branch as the fruit, are unmistakable. Holly berries are smooth and hard, among prickly leaves.

species.name: Baobab (fruit and leaves)
species.habitat: Hot, dry savanna and open woodland on stony, well-drained, frost-free ground, from the Sahel to the Limpopo valley; often a lone giant beside a village, a field or a pan.
species.identify: A vast, swollen grey trunk with smooth, folded bark and stubby branches that look like roots, bare of leaves for most of the dry season. The leaves are hand-shaped, with five to seven finger-like leaflets. The fruit is a velvety, egg- to sausage-shaped pod up to 25 cm (10 in) long on a long hanging stalk: a hard woody shell around chalky, off-white pulp and black kidney-shaped seeds.
species.use: Take fruit only when the shell is dry and brown and the seeds rattle inside. Crack it open and suck the tart, sherbet-like pulp off the seeds, or soak the pulp in water and strain it for a lemony drink; it also goes into porridge. Young leaves, picked in the rains, are cooked as a relish or dried and powdered for soup across West Africa. Knock fruit down with a hooked pole — don't climb the tree.
species.lookalikes: No other tree looks like a baobab. Sausage tree (Kigelia) also dangles fruit on long cords, but its 'sausages' are huge, heavy and solid, with no dry shell full of powder. Take pods only from a tree you have seen.
species.caution: Baobab is a protected tree in South Africa: no cutting, bark-stripping or damage without a licence, though a household may take a small share of the fruit. In the Sahel, heavy use of the fruit has been cited among the pressures on the trees — take a little from many trees rather than everything from one.

species.name: Marula
species.habitat: Low-lying bushveld and open woodland — the Lowveld, Limpopo, northern KwaZulu-Natal, Zimbabwe, Mozambique and north-central Namibia — and left standing in fields and around homesteads for its fruit.
species.identify: A single-stemmed tree with a broad, spreading crown and grey, mottled bark. Leaves are divided into pairs of leaflets with one at the tip, bunched at the ends of the branches. The plum-sized fruits, 3–4 cm (1½ in) long, fall while still green and turn pale yellow on the ground; inside is white, juicy flesh around a hard, thick-walled stone holding two or three kernels. Only female trees bear fruit.
species.use: Gather the yellow fallen fruit, bite through the tough skin and suck out the tart, aromatic flesh, or make jelly and juice. Fermented for a few days the juice becomes marula beer — mukumbi to the Vhavenda, omaongo to the Ovambo of northern Namibia. The kernels are rich and nutty, but prising them out of the stone takes practice.
species.lookalikes: No dangerous double is known. Look up before you pick up: the tree above should have the bunched, divided leaves, and the fruit a hard stone with plugged holes, not a soft pit or many small seeds.
species.caution: Marula is a protected tree in South Africa. Collect fruit for the household; don't cut or damage the tree, and selling the fruit needs a licence. Fallen fruit starts to ferment within days in the heat.

species.name: Tamarind
species.habitat: Dry savanna, riverbanks and village squares from Senegal to Sudan and down the east of the continent; a favourite shade tree, often very old.
species.identify: A big, dense, evergreen tree with feathery leaves of many small paired leaflets (no single leaflet at the tip) and small yellow flowers streaked with orange or red. The fruit is a brown, slightly curved pod with a thin, brittle shell over sticky, brown, sweet-sour pulp and one to six glossy brown seeds; African pods are the short kind.
species.use: Crack the shell and eat the pulp off the seeds, or soak a handful in water, strain and sweeten it: tamarind drinks are made from Sudan and Egypt across West Africa and down the East African coast. A little goes into porridge. Young leaves, flowers and baby pods are pleasantly sour and used as seasoning.
species.lookalikes: Other savanna pods are the confusion. A tamarind pod has a thin, brittle, cinnamon-brown shell that cracks under your thumb over sticky pulp; pods that are woody, flat, papery or hairy belong to something else.
species.caution: The pulp is laxative in quantity. The seeds are edible only after soaking and boiling.

species.name: Monkey orange (green monkey orange)
species.habitat: Dry woodland, bushveld, sandy riverbanks, sand forest and coastal bush from sea level to about 1,800 m; the fruit comes after good rains.
species.identify: A small, often spiny tree with opposite, rounded, glossy leaves showing three to five veins running from the base. The fruit is large, round and hard, with a woody shell that turns from green (often speckled) to yellow as it ripens; inside, many hard brown seeds packed in sweet-sour, brown, edible pulp.
species.use: Crack a ripe, yellow fruit and eat the pulp off the seeds, or mash it with water for juice. Green fruit can be picked and left to ripen: the Basarwa (San) of Botswana bury it in sand for months, and it comes out juicy and golden. Spit the seeds out — don't chew them.
species.lookalikes: Several monkey oranges share the woodland. The spine-leaved monkey orange (S. pungens) and corky-bark monkey orange (S. cocculoides) are eaten too. Strychnos is the genus of strychnine, though, so eat only the ripe pulp of a tree someone has shown you.
species.caution: The seeds and unripe fruit are poisonous; unripe flesh causes vomiting. Eat only the pulp of fully yellow fruit.

species.name: Sycamore fig
species.habitat: Rich soils along rivers, streams, swamps and waterholes in the savanna, and riverine woodland; often the giant shade tree on the bank.
species.identify: A big, spreading tree with yellowish to orange bark that peels in papery strips, and rough, heart-shaped leaves with prominent yellow veins beneath. The figs, 2–3 cm (about 1 in) across, grow in thick clusters on short leafless branchlets from the trunk and main branches and ripen from greenish-buff to yellow or reddish. Broken twigs bleed milky latex.
species.use: Eat ripe, soft figs fresh, stewed or dried. Break each open first: wild figs are pollinated from the inside by tiny wasps, and often hold them. They are less sweet than a garden fig.
species.lookalikes: Africa has dozens of wild figs, all with milky sap and figs of some kind. Learn this one by its peeling yellow-orange bark and big clusters of figs on the trunk, and eat only from a tree you have identified.
species.caution: The milky latex irritates skin and eyes.

species.name: Shea fruit
species.habitat: The Guinea and Sudan savanna belt from Senegal to Sudan, western Ethiopia and northern Uganda; left standing in farmers' fields as 'shea parkland'.
species.identify: A medium-sized tree with thick, corky bark deeply cracked into squares, white latex where it is cut, and long, leathery, oblong leaves crowded in tufts at the branch tips. The fruit looks like a large plum, 4–8 cm (1½–3 in) long, with a thin layer of sweet green pulp around one big, glossy brown seed — the shea 'nut'.
species.use: Gather ripe fruit from the ground and eat the sweet pulp fresh — in moderation, as it is mildly laxative. The kernels make shea butter: roasted, pounded, boiled and skimmed, traditionally by women, and used for cooking across West Africa.
species.lookalikes: No dangerous double is known. Collect fallen fruit rather than picking: ripening and fully ripe fruit are hard to tell apart on the tree.
species.caution: Rights to the fruit depend on who holds the land; in shea country it is traditionally gathered by women and children. Uganda has banned cutting shea trees.

species.name: African star apple (agbalumo, udara)
species.habitat: Lowland forest and farm-forest in West and Central Africa — Nigeria, Ghana, Côte d'Ivoire, Cameroon — mostly from trees kept in farms and villages.
species.identify: A forest tree with milky latex. The fruit is round with a smooth skin that ripens from green to orange, yellowish-peach or burnt orange; cut across, the seeds sit in a five-pointed star in sticky, sweet-sour pulp.
species.use: Break open a ripe fruit and eat the sweet, sticky flesh; the skin is chewable and many people eat it too, chewing it like gum. Spit out the seeds.
species.lookalikes: Its close relative Gambeya africana is eaten the same way. No dangerous double is known, but in the forest, never eat an unfamiliar fruit just because it has milky sap — so do many poisonous ones.
species.caution: The sticky latex gums up lips and fingers.

species.name: Desert date (balanites)
species.habitat: Woodland and scrub along the Sahara's southern edge from the Atlantic to the Red Sea, and the dry country of the Nile, the Horn and East Africa; it shrugs off sand, clay, floods, fire and goats.
species.identify: A spiny tree up to about 10 m with long, straight, green spines arranged in a spiral, and dark green leaves of two small leaflets growing from the base of the spines. The date-like fruit is under 4 cm (1½ in) long, green when unripe, ripening yellow to pale brown, with a brittle skin over sticky, bittersweet pulp and one very hard stone.
species.use: Eat ripe fruit raw, or sun-dry it and store it like dates; the pulp is soaked for a drink or stirred into porridge. Young leaves and tender shoots are boiled and eaten as a vegetable. The oily kernel inside the stone is food only after long processing to remove its bitterness.
species.lookalikes: No dangerous double is known. The green spines with leaflets growing from their base are unmistakable.
species.caution: The kernel, bark and fruit contain saponins — laxative, and potent enough that extracts kill bilharzia snails and stun fish. Eat the pulp in moderation and never the raw kernel. The spines are razor-sharp.

species.name: Eru (okazi, fumbwa)
species.habitat: Humid rainforest, secondary forest and forest edges from Nigeria and Cameroon to Gabon, the Congos and Angola, from sea level to 1,200 m; a shade-loving climber on middle- and understorey trees.
species.identify: A slender climbing vine up to about 10 m long with thick, glossy, leathery, oval leaves about 8 cm (3 in) long, pointed at the tip. It is a gymnosperm, related to the conifers: no true flowers, but small cone-like spikes, and on female vines fleshy seeds 1–1.5 cm long that ripen red-orange.
species.use: Take leaves or side shoots and leave the vine to regrow. Shred the tough leaves into very fine strips and cook them in soup or stew — eru soup in Cameroon, okazi and afang soup in Nigeria — often with waterleaf to soften them. Shredded leaves can be dried to keep.
species.lookalikes: Many forest climbers have glossy, leathery leaves, and some are deadly — Strophanthus, a source of African arrow poison, is one. Pick eru only from a vine someone has shown you; otherwise buy it in the market, where it is sold all year.
species.caution: Wild eru has been badly over-harvested: pulling whole stems from trees, and felling trees to reach them, destroys stands. Take side shoots only.

species.name: Amaranth greens (morogo, mchicha)
species.habitat: Fields, gardens, field edges and freshly disturbed, fertile ground; it comes up with the rains, and in many places farmers spare it while weeding.
species.identify: Upright or sprawling herbs, often with reddish stems, carrying alternate, oval to diamond-shaped, smooth-edged leaves on long stalks, and dense, bristly spikes of tiny green or reddish flowers at the top and in the leaf joints. No milky sap, no berries, no trumpet flowers. Spiny amaranth has a pair of sharp spines at each leaf base.
species.use: Pick young leaves and tips before the plant flowers. Cook them like spinach in plenty of water, pour the water off, then add them to stews, peanut sauce or relish to eat with pap or ugali — the way morogo is eaten in South Africa and mchicha in East Africa. Cutting the tops makes the plant branch and give more.
species.lookalikes: Thorn apple (Datura) seedlings come up in the same maize fields and gardens and can kill: their leaves are larger, with coarse, irregular teeth, and smell rank when crushed, and the plant soon carries big white or purple trumpet flowers and a spiny seed pod. Nightshades (Solanum) have star-shaped flowers and berries. Amaranth has neither — only bristly flower spikes.
species.caution: Amaranth stores nitrate, mostly in the stems, and oxalate like other leafy greens; cooking in ample water and throwing the water away takes out much of both. Avoid plants from heavily manured or sprayed fields, roadsides and rubbish tips.

species.name: Spider plant (cat's whiskers)
species.habitat: Near homes and fields on fertile, well-drained ground from sea level to 2,400 m; a weed of well-manured crops, often spared or sown on purpose.
species.identify: An upright, branching annual up to about 1.5 m with a sticky, glandular stem and a strong smell. Leaves are hand-shaped, of three to seven (usually five) finely toothed leaflets. The flowers are white or purple-tinged with four clawed petals, and the purple stamens and the ovary are held out on a long stalk well beyond the petals — the cat's whiskers. Pods are long, thin and beaked.
species.use: Pick tender leaves and shoot tips and cook them. They can be bitter, so many cooks boil them and pour off the water, or cook them with milk, peanut paste or milder greens such as amaranth and cowpea leaves. Leaves are also blanched and sun-dried, as balls or powder, for the dry season — omuvanda cakes in Namibia.
species.lookalikes: Other spider-flowers (Cleome species) grow in the same places, and a few are eaten locally too; only this one carries its stamens and ovary on a long stalk far beyond the petals. If you can't see the 'whiskers', wait for it to flower.
species.caution: The sticky hairs can irritate skin. The seeds are acrid with mustard-oil compounds and have been thrown into water to kill fish; eat the cooked leaves, not the seeds.

species.name: Num-num (Natal plum)
species.habitat: Coastal bush, coastal forest and dunes from Humansdorp in the Eastern Cape north through KwaZulu-Natal to Mozambique; planted widely as a spiny, salt-proof hedge.
species.identify: A dense, evergreen shrub with glossy, leathery, dark green leaves in opposite pairs, sharp forked (Y-shaped) thorns, and white milky sap from any broken leaf or twig. Flowers are white five-petalled stars, scented most strongly at night. The fruit is a large, oval, glossy red berry with soft red flesh; flowers and fruit are often on the bush together.
species.use: Eat ripe, deep-red fruit raw, or cook it into jam or jelly. It is rich in vitamin C. Pick only fruit that is fully red and gives slightly; the ripe skin bruises easily.
species.lookalikes: Dune poison-bush (Acokanthera oblongifolia) grows in the same coastal bush from the Eastern Cape to KwaZulu-Natal, belongs to the same family, has sweet-scented white flowers, and bears red fruit that ripens to purple-black — and every part of it, the fruit included, is poisonous to the heart. It has no forked thorns. No Y-shaped thorns, no picking.
species.caution: Check for the forked thorns on every bush before you pick, and eat only the red fruit — not the leaves, stems or sap. Num-num belongs to the Apocynaceae, a family protected in the Western Cape under Schedule 4 of the Nature Conservation Ordinance: picking from wild plants there needs a CapeNature permit as well as the landowner's consent; garden and hedge plants are another matter.

species.name: Sour fig (suurvy)
species.habitat: Coastal and inland slopes, dunes and bare, disturbed sandy ground from Namaqualand through the Western Cape to the Eastern Cape; a creeping pioneer that mats over open ground.
species.identify: Trailing mats of fat, three-angled, finger-like succulent leaves, often reddish at the tips. Big many-petalled flowers 6–15 cm (2½–6 in) across, yellow and fading to pale pink. The fruit is a fleshy, top-shaped capsule about 35 mm (1⅜ in) across that turns from green to yellow and smells sweet when ripe.
species.use: Pick ripe yellow fruit, nip off the base and suck out the sticky, salty-sour pulp with its tiny seeds. Sour figs are best once they have dried and wrinkled, eaten as they are or cooked into the Cape's famously tart sour-fig jam.
species.lookalikes: Other Carpobrotus are edible too, and sweeter: ghaukum (C. deliciosus) and elandsvy (C. quadrifidus). Most other vygies have small, dry seed capsules; only Carpobrotus makes the big, fleshy, top-shaped fruit.
species.caution: Puff adders and Cape cobras lie up in the mats to ambush the rodents that come for the fruit — look before you reach in. In the Western Cape every member of the vygie family (Mesembryanthemaceae), sour fig included, is protected under Schedule 4 of the Nature Conservation Ordinance: picking needs a permit from CapeNature as well as the landowner's consent.

species.name: Waterblommetjie (Cape pondweed)
species.habitat: Seasonal ponds and vleis 1–2 m deep in the winter-rainfall Cape, which often dry out in summer; farmed in dams for the market.
species.identify: Long-stalked, narrow-oval leaves floating flat on the water, and above them forked white flower spikes shaped like a 'Y', each branch lined with white petal-like bracts and dark purple-brown stamens, sweetly scented. The plant dies back as the pools dry in summer and regrows with the autumn rain.
species.use: Pick the flower heads and buds, wash them well and cook them — above all in waterblommetjiebredie, the Cape stew of mutton or lamb, onions and potatoes, often with a few leaves of wild sorrel.
species.lookalikes: Nothing else in a Cape vlei carries a forked, white, scented flower spike above floating leaves.
species.caution: Most waterblommetjies sold are farmed, and nobody knows what wild picking does to the plant. In the wild, pick only with the landowner's permission, never in a reserve, and only from clean water: the plant is sensitive to herbicides and pesticides, and vleis by farms and roads collect run-off.

species.name: Kei apple
species.habitat: Valley bushveld, dry woodland, wooded grassland and forest edges from the Eastern Cape through KwaZulu-Natal and Eswatini to Limpopo and Zimbabwe; planted everywhere as an impenetrable hedge.
species.identify: A dense, viciously thorny shrub or small tree with straight spines 3–6 cm (1–2½ in) long and clusters of small oval leaves at their base. Male and female flowers are on separate plants, so only some bushes fruit. The fruit is a round, apricot-coloured berry 2.5–4 cm (1–1½ in) across, the same yellow-orange inside and out, with several small seeds.
species.use: Pick fully coloured, slightly soft fruit in midsummer. It is very sour, so eat it with sugar, or make the excellent jam and jelly it is known for; it is acidic enough to pickle without vinegar.
species.lookalikes: Wild Solanum shrubs — bitter apple and its relatives — carry yellow, poisonous, Kei-apple-sized fruit in the same bushveld. They are soft-wooded shrubs, often with prickles on the leaves themselves and purple or white star-shaped flowers. A Kei apple is a woody tree or hedge armed with long, straight thorns on the branches.
species.caution: Gloves and long sleeves: the thorns go deep.

species.name: Wild garlic (Tulbaghia)
species.habitat: Grassland and rocky places in the Eastern Cape, KwaZulu-Natal and Limpopo, north to Zimbabwe; also a very common garden and pavement plant in South Africa.
species.identify: Clumps of narrow, grey-green, strap-like leaves up to about 60 cm (2 ft), and on bare stalks above them loose heads of tubular lilac-mauve flowers from midsummer into autumn. Leaves and flowers smell strongly of garlic when bruised — and that smell is the test.
species.use: Snip leaves and flowers and use them like chives or garlic: in salads, with potatoes and meat, or cooked as a green. Zulu cooks eat them as a spinach and as a hot, peppery seasoning. Leave the bulb in the ground.
species.lookalikes: Agapanthus is often planted beside it and has similar strap leaves, but broader, glossier and with no garlic smell; it is not eaten. In the veld, several bulbs with grassy or strap-shaped leaves are poisonous — chincherinchees (Ornithogalum) among them — and none smells of garlic. Crush a leaf every time: no garlic smell, no picking.
species.caution: Eat the leaves and flowers. The bulb is a traditional medicine, and deaths and severe gut poisoning have been linked to medicines made from the plant, probably in large doses.

species.name: Termite mushrooms (omajowa)
species.habitat: On and around the mounds of fungus-farming termites (Macrotermes and their relatives) in savanna, woodland and fields, right after soaking rains.
species.identify: It grows out of a termite mound or the ground over a termite nest, never from wood. The cap usually has a pointed nipple at its centre, and the stem tapers into a long, tough root (pseudorhiza) that runs down — sometimes a metre or more — to the termites' fungus garden. Sizes run from a few centimetres (Termitomyces microcarpus, in crowds) to frying-pan caps of 15–40 cm (T. schimperi) and, in T. titanicus, up to a metre across.
species.use: Dig beside the stem until you can see the root going down into the nest — that root is the identification — then cut the mushroom and leave the rest; the same mound can fruit again for years. Cook them the same day — fried, stewed, or treated like steak.
species.lookalikes: Deadly Amanitas come up in the same woodland after rain: they rise from a swollen bulb or a sac-like cup at the base, have white gills and often a ring, and have no long root into a termite nest. The green-spored parasol (Chlorophyllum molybdites) is big, pale and scaly, grows in grass, and has poisoned many people in Asia who took it for a termite mushroom; it has a ring and drops a green spore print. Death cap has reached South Africa and grows in cool, moist plantations.
species.caution: If you can't see the root going down into a termite nest, it is not a termite mushroom. If you are new to them, buy from people who gather them every season.

species.name: Kalahari truffle
species.habitat: Deep Kalahari sand in Botswana, eastern Namibia and the Northern Cape, among grasses, Grewia bushes, acacias and wild tsamma melons, after a good rainy season.
species.identify: A roundish, potato-like fungus growing just under the sand, up to 12 cm (4¾ in) across and usually under 200 g (7 oz). It gives itself away by lifting the sand into a little mound with cracks in the surface. Cut through, it is solid right through — no gills, no stem, no hollow.
species.use: Brush off the sand, peel and cook — sliced and fried or in a stew. Take a few from each patch and leave the rest.
species.lookalikes: Earthballs (Scleroderma) also grow as round lumps in sand: they have a thick, hard rind and turn purple-black inside, and they cause violent sickness. A young Amanita 'egg' cut in half shows the outline of a cap and stem. A Kalahari truffle has no rind like that and no cap or stem inside — it is solid right through.
species.caution: A traditional food of the Khoisan peoples of the Kalahari, and now also sold. Populations are thought to be declining — harvest lightly.

species.name: Sorrel (suring)
species.habitat: Roadsides and grassy places through the winter-rainfall Cape, Namaqualand and Namibia, where it is very common. It grows from small bulbs, comes up with the autumn rain and dies back to the bulbs in the dry summer.
species.identify: A low, almost stemless plant with clover-like leaves of three heart-shaped leaflets, each notched at the tip, on long stalks. Bright yellow, funnel-shaped flowers with a whitish tube stand above the leaves in loose heads of three to twenty on bare stalks, from about June to October. Leaves and stalks taste sharply sour.
species.use: Snap off leaves and juicy flower stalks and leave the bulbs. Cape children chew the stalks for their sour juice; cooks use leaves and stalks as a souring herb in waterblommetjiebredie and other winter stews, or in a pot of dune spinach with butter. Surings boiled in milk were once a favourite breakfast.
species.lookalikes: The Cape has many other wild Oxalis; suring is the common bright-yellow one of roadsides, flowering in winter. Clover has rounded, unnotched leaflets and no yellow funnel flowers.
species.caution: Rich in oxalic acid, like every sorrel: a seasoning, not a plateful. Hungry livestock that gorge on it have died of oxalate poisoning. In the Western Cape, picking on land that is not yours needs the owner's written permission, and picking within 90 m of the centre of a public road needs a permit.

species.name: Dune spinach (duinespinasie)
species.habitat: Coastal and estuarine sand dunes from southern Namibia round the Cape to the Eastern Cape, often among the first plants on moist, moving foredunes.
species.identify: A sprawling, trailing undershrub with thick, pale stems and fat, oval, saddle-shaped leaves 1–6 cm (½–2½ in) long that sit straight on the stem without a stalk and glisten as if wet — the sheen comes from tiny water-storage cells. Small yellow four-petalled flowers sit in groups of three to five in the upper leaf joints from August to November, followed by thickly four-winged fruit.
species.use: Pick the soft new tips and leafy stems that grow in the rainy season, and wash out every grain of sand. Boil or steam them like spinach; the flavour is mild, so the Cape way is to cook them with a little suring and finish with butter. The texture is slightly grainy. Raw leaves are crisp and salty in a salad.
species.lookalikes: No dangerous double is known. Other succulents share the dunes, so learn it with the yellow four-petalled flowers or the four-winged fruit on the plant.
species.caution: Its close relative New Zealand spinach holds oxalates and is blanched before cooking; doing the same here is a sensible precaution. Take a few tips from each plant and never pull plants up: dune spinach binds moving sand. Much of the Cape coast is reserve or national park, where picking is not allowed; elsewhere in the Western Cape the landowner's written permission is required.

species.name: Cape gooseberry (golden berry)
species.habitat: An escape from gardens and farms that has run wild across much of South Africa, from the Cape to KwaZulu-Natal, the Lowveld and the Highveld, and in the East African highlands spreads as a harmless weed of gardens, fields, secondary scrub and abandoned plantations.
species.identify: A soft, spreading, velvety-hairy shrub up to about 1 m (3 ft) with heart-shaped, wavy-edged leaves. The drooping, bell-shaped flowers, 1–2 cm (½–¾ in) across, are yellow with dark purple-brown blotches inside. Each fruit is a smooth, round, golden-orange berry 1.25–2 cm (½–¾ in) across, like a tiny tomato, enclosed in a papery, ten-ribbed husk — a small lantern — that dries from green to straw-brown.
species.use: Pick when the husk has dried to a papery straw colour and the berry inside is fully golden. Peel back the husk and eat the sweet-sharp berry fresh, or cook it into jam, long a South African staple. Left in their husks, the berries travel and keep better.
species.lookalikes: Wild nightshades (Solanum) with poisonous berries grow in the same places; none wraps its fruit in a papery lantern. No husk, no picking — and inside the husk, only a golden berry.
species.caution: Unripe fruit, leaves, stems and flowers contain solanine and related alkaloids and are poisonous. Eat only fully ripe, golden berries.

species.name: Wild rosemary (kapokbos)
species.habitat: Clay and granite slopes, coastal scrub and dry veld through the Western and Eastern Cape and Namaqualand; one of the commonest shrubs of the Cape.
species.identify: A bushy, evergreen, silvery-grey shrub up to about 1 m (3 ft) with small, narrow, needle-like leaves in tufts along the branches — fleshier on plants near the sea — that smell of camphor, like Vicks, when crushed. In autumn and winter it covers itself in small flowers of two or three white petals round a purple centre, followed by seed heads wrapped in long white hairs like cotton wool: kapok is the Afrikaans for snow.
species.use: Use a sprig in cooking as you would garden rosemary, and sparingly. For the traditional tea, long taken for coughs, colds and colic, steep one sprig in a cup of boiling water. Snip sprigs with scissors and leave the bush to regrow.
species.lookalikes: Southern Africa has 34 species of Eriocephalus, all with woolly seed heads, and many small grey shrubs look alike out of flower. Pick only from a bush that smells strongly of camphor when crushed and that you have seen in flower or in seed.
species.caution: A herb, not a vegetable. SANBI's monograph records no known side effects, but 'none known' is not proof of safety: it is a traditional diuretic and a remedy for women's complaints, so avoid medicinal amounts in pregnancy. Like many daisy-family plants it contains sesquiterpene lactones, which can irritate sensitive skin. In the Western Cape, picking needs the landowner's written permission, and a permit within 90 m of a public road; never pick in a reserve.

species.name: Mussels (rock mussels)
species.latin: Mytilus spp., Choromytilus meridionalis, Perna perna
species.habitat: Dense beds on wave-washed rocks, piers and harbour walls from the middle shore down into the shallows, reached on low spring tides. In South Africa, the black mussel and the introduced Mediterranean mussel cover the West and South coasts and the brown mussel the South and East coasts; in Europe, the blue and Mediterranean mussels; in North America, the blue mussel on the Atlantic and its Pacific relatives in the west.
species.identify: Paired, wedge-shaped shells, pointed at the hinge end and rounded at the other, anchored in clusters by tough threads (the byssus, or beard). Blue and Mediterranean mussels are blue-black, purple or brownish and grow to about 14 cm (5½ in); the Cape's black mussel is narrower, glossier and blacker; the brown mussel is brown.
species.use: Gather at low tide on clean, open coast, by hand or with a blunt blade (in South Africa, no wider than 12 mm). species.name: Sea lettuce
species.habitat: On rocks, in pools and on other seaweeds at every level of the shore and into the shallows, in estuaries and harbours too. It grows most lushly where the water is rich in nutrients.
species.identify: Bright to dark green, translucent, crumpled sheets up to about 30 cm (12 in) across and only two cells thick — like wet green tissue paper — fixed by a tiny disc, with no stalk.
species.use: Cut fresh, attached, bright green sheets from clean water and rinse them well. Eat them raw in salads or simmer them in soups, as the Scots do. In Wales it goes into laverbread, and in Japan and Korea it is eaten with rice.
species.lookalikes: The risk is not a look-alike but the water: a thick, lush mat of sea lettuce is a sign of nutrient-rich, often polluted water, not of clean water.
species.caution: Take only attached, healthy sheets from clean, open coast — never from harbours, near outfalls or from drifts on the beach. Rotting heaps of green seaweed give off hydrogen sulphide, a toxic gas that caused deaths during the 2009 blooms in Brittany. In South Africa, collecting any seaweed needs a permit, and Namibia has its own rules; Washington State requires a licence; California sets a daily limit and closes marine protected areas; elsewhere, reserves and some states and provinces have their own rules. Cut with scissors and leave the base.

species.name: Sea bamboo (Cape kelp)
species.habitat: The kelp forests of the cold Atlantic coast, from the south of South Africa round the Cape Peninsula and up the West Coast into Namibia, in shallow water to about 8 m (26 ft). After storms, whole plants wash up on the beaches.
species.identify: South Africa's largest kelp, up to 12–15 m (40–50 ft) long: a root-like holdfast, a single long, hollow, gas-filled stalk and, at the surface, a large bulb carrying a tangle of thick, strap-like fronds. Washed up, it lies on the sand like brown hosepipe with a bulb at one end.
species.use: Cape foragers wash it well in fresh water, then pickle it or cook it into dishes such as kelp lasagne and falafel. Use it in small amounts, as a seasoning rather than a vegetable.
species.lookalikes: Split-fan kelp (Laminaria pallida), the other big kelp of the West Coast, has no floating bulb; it is harvested commercially too.
species.caution: Very high in iodine, like all brown kelps. France's food-safety agency advises people with thyroid, heart or kidney disease, and pregnant or breastfeeding women without medical advice, not to eat it, and says there are too few data to judge the risk for children. In South Africa, collecting any seaweed needs a permit: the coast is divided into commercial seaweed concession areas whose rules cover washed-up kelp as well as living plants. Ask DFFE before you take any; in Namibia, ask the fisheries ministry.

species.name: Rock samphire (sea fennel)
species.habitat: Sea cliffs, rocks, old sea walls, sand and shingle within reach of the spray, rooting deep into cracks: from Ireland and Britain down the Atlantic coast, and round the Mediterranean and the Black Sea.
species.identify: A hairless, cushion-forming perennial 15–50 cm (6–20 in) tall with ridged, solid stems and very fleshy, grey-green leaves divided into narrow, almost cylindrical lobes; crushed, they smell resinous and lemony. Flat umbels of small yellow-green flowers from June to September are followed by spongy, ribbed, egg-shaped fruit.
species.use: Pick young leaves and shoot tips in spring and early summer, before it flowers. Blanch them briefly or pickle them in vinegar; on Italy's Conero coast it is the antipasto paccasassi. A few raw leaves are sharply aromatic in a salad.
species.lookalikes: Marsh samphire shares the name but is a leafless, jointed plant of salt-marsh mud. Rock samphire's fleshy, divided leaves on a cliff are distinctive.
species.caution: Pick only what you can reach safely; in King Lear, Shakespeare called gathering samphire on the cliffs of Dover a 'dreadful trade'. Cut, never uproot — in Britain, uprooting any wild plant without authorisation is an offence — and leave it alone in protected areas: the Calanques National Park near Marseille asks visitors to look, not touch.

species.name: Carrageen (Irish moss)
species.habitat: Rocks and pools on the middle and lower shore and down to about 24 m (80 ft), on both sides of the North Atlantic: from Iceland and Norway to Spain, and from Labrador to New Jersey.
species.identify: A small, tough, springy red seaweed up to about 22 cm (9 in), in tufts from a disc-shaped holdfast. A narrow, unbranched stalk widens into flat fronds that fork up to five times into a fan with rounded tips. The colour runs from deep purple-red to green or yellow in strong sun, and under water the tips often shine blue-violet.
species.use: Cut tufts at low spring tides and leave the holdfast. Rinse and dry it; dried carrageen is brown and crisp and unfurls as soon as it is wet. Simmer a small handful in milk for about 20 minutes, strain, sweeten and leave to set: carrageen moss pudding, the Irish blancmange. It thickens soups and jellies the same way.
species.lookalikes: False Irish moss (Mastocarpus stellatus) grows in the same places: its fronds are channelled and often twisted, with thickened edges and its reproductive bodies in small, pimple-like bumps on the surface. Carrageen's fronds are flat.
species.caution: Cut, don't pull, and take it only from clean, open shores, away from outfalls and harbours. Like all seaweeds it contains iodine: eat it in modest amounts, and ask a doctor first if you have a thyroid condition or are pregnant. Check local rules; some states and provinces license seaweed harvest.

species.name: Sea purslane
species.habitat: The drier parts of salt marshes and the edges of tidal creeks and pools, often lining the creeks in low, silvery hedges that the highest tides cover; also coastal dunes.
species.identify: A low, straggling, much-branched shrub up to about 80 cm (2½ ft) on sprawling, woody stems. The leaves are thick, untoothed and oval to elliptical, in opposite pairs, silvery grey-green and mealy to the touch. From July to September, short spikes of tiny greyish flowers with yellow stamens appear at the tips.
species.use: Pick the tender leaves and tips: they are crunchy and naturally salty. Eat them raw in salads, steam or fry them briefly to go with fish, add them to soups in place of salt, or pickle them.
species.lookalikes: Young plants can be confused with sea-blite, which is also eaten. Despite the name it is no relation of purslane (Portulaca), the garden weed.
species.caution: Watch the tide and the soft mud of the creeks. Pick away from outfalls, and remember that many salt marshes are protected: in Britain, uprooting any wild plant without authorisation is an offence, and many marshes are Sites of Special Scientific Interest.

species.name: Alexanders
species.habitat: Road verges, hedge banks, cliff tops and cliff paths, field margins, scrub and waste ground, most of all near the sea in Britain and Ireland, where it was probably brought by the Romans; common through central and southern Europe and around the Mediterranean, its home.
species.identify: A stout, hairless biennial up to 1.5 m (5 ft). The glossy, yellowish- to dark green leaves are divided into broad, bluntly toothed leaflets, and the stems are solid when young, becoming hollow and grooved with age. From April to June it carries dense, rounded umbels of yellow-green flowers with no sepals, followed by seeds that turn from green to black in July and August.
species.use: Cut the succulent stems from February; they are at their best as the first flower buds appear in late March and April. Peel and steam or boil them like asparagus and toss in butter. Leaves and flowers go into salads, and every part is edible — the fleshy roots were once dug in winter. It was a common pot-herb until celery displaced it in the 18th century.
species.lookalikes: Hemlock water-dropwort shares its family and can grow nearby; in Britain most recorded poisonings by it have been fatal. It has white flowers, finely divided, flat leaves that smell deceptively of parsley or celery, and grows in wet ground. Hemlock, also white-flowered, has ferny leaves and purple-blotched stems. Alexanders' flowers are yellow-green; before they open, learn the plant with someone who knows it.
species.caution: The danger is in the identification, above all in late winter and early spring, when the stems are picked before the flowers open. Never dig roots to eat unless the plant is unmistakable — hemlock water-dropwort's roots, mistaken for parsnips, cause the worst poisonings.

species.name: Caper
species.habitat: Old stone walls, rock crevices, cliffs and dry, stony slopes, often by the sea, all round the Mediterranean.
species.identify: A sprawling shrub with long, trailing stems, thick, shiny, round to oval leaves and usually small curved thorns. The showy flowers last a single day: four white to pinkish petals and a burst of long violet stamens. Before they open they are small, round green buds — the capers. Left on the plant, they become plump green fruit on long stalks, the caper berries.
species.use: Pick unopened buds in the morning, the smaller the better, and come back to the same bush often. Raw buds are not eaten: dry them in the sun, then cure them in brine, coarse salt, or salt and vinegar, which releases their mustard flavour. Caper berries are pickled the same way.
species.lookalikes: A few poisonous species of Capparis elsewhere in the world look similar, so pick only a plant you know as Capparis spinosa.
species.caution: Don't damage old walls and monuments, where the plant often roots. Many coastal cliffs and islands are protected: in Italy's national parks, for example, collecting wild plants is forbidden outside farmed land unless the park's own rules allow it.

species.name: Carob (St John's bread)
species.habitat: Warm, dry, frost-free hills and coastal plains around the Mediterranean, in maquis, open woodland and old terraced groves; wild in the east and long naturalised in the west.
species.identify: A broad, round-crowned evergreen tree up to 15 m (50 ft) with leaves 10–20 cm (4–8 in) long, divided into pairs of leaflets. Small flowers grow straight from the trunk and old branches in autumn. The pods are flat, leathery and slightly curved, 10–30 cm (4–12 in) long, ripening from green to dark brown, sweet-smelling, with 10–13 very hard seeds. Most trees are male or female, and only females bear pods.
species.use: Take pods when they are dark brown and dry, before the winter rains; they are traditionally shaken or knocked down with a long hooked pole. Chew the sweet pulp straight from the pod and spit out the seeds, roast and grind the pods into a cocoa-like flour, or boil the ground pods into a thick, honey-like syrup.
species.lookalikes: Identify the tree as well as the pod: divided leaves, flowers on the trunk, and pods with rock-hard seeds.
species.caution: Many carobs stand in owned groves and on farm terraces: ask before you take pods. The pods hold up to 1.5% tannins, which hinder the digestion of protein in quantity; don't try to eat the seeds. In protected areas such as Italy's national parks, collecting plants is forbidden outside farmed land unless the park allows it.

species.name: Myrtle (mirto)
species.habitat: Maquis, scrub and open woodland, mostly near the coast and below about 800 m (2,600 ft), on neutral to slightly acid soils all round the Mediterranean.
species.identify: A dense evergreen shrub up to 5 m (16 ft) with small leaves 2–5 cm (¾–2 in) long in opposite pairs, fragrant with essential oil when crushed. Its white or pink-tinged flowers have five petals and a brush of many stamens. The berries change colour in late summer and ripen from November into the new year to blue-black.
species.use: Pick fully ripe, blue-black berries by hand, without cutting the shoots. In Sardinia, ripe berries macerated in alcohol make red mirto, and the leaves white mirto.
species.lookalikes: Laurustinus (Viburnum tinus), another common maquis shrub with leaves in opposite pairs, has metallic blue-black berries that have been used as a purgative; its leaves are much larger, 4–10 cm (1½–4 in). Crush a leaf: no myrtle scent, no picking.
species.caution: Strip berries only: cutting whole shoots, as many pickers do, puts the bushes under heavy pressure. In Italy's national parks collecting plants is forbidden outside farmed land unless the park allows it, and other protected areas have their own rules.
